This approach enables both the quantification of entanglement and the distinction between quantum discord and entangled phases under different environmental conditions. Specifically, we analyze environments comprising two atoms and one or two photons, with atoms and photons potentially exhibiting quantum correlations prior to interacting with the 2-qubit quantum computer. Numerical simulations were conducted for scenarios involving two atoms with zero, one, or two photons, accounting for cases where individual pairs or all three pairs may be correlated with the 2-qubit computer. We examined three types of light-matter interactions: Rayleigh, Raman, and QED. Our findings indicate that in the Rayleigh case, maximal entanglement is preserved only when the system involves two atoms with no photons. In the Raman case, correlations between the two atoms in the environment significantly suppress entanglement; otherwise, the system remains entangled provided the initial state contains one or zero photons. Regarding the QED case, if at least one atom is excited, entanglement decreases; if both atoms are in ground states, the system stays entangled unless two photons are present. These results offer valuable insights for future experiments. Furthermore, our study highlights the critical influence of light-matter interactions, suggesting that carefully engineering these interactions could effectively manage the entanglement of quantum computers. This paves the way for developing novel architectures for quantum computing. (Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China.) This study advances the field of misinformation detection by introducing a novel dataset comprising English tweet comments, comprising 1,000 instances each of legitimate and manipulated content. In this framework, synaptic connections are modeled as random variables where pre- and postsynaptic neurons are selected randomly and independently, adhering to a degree distribution $P_{\rm K}(k)$. Initially, we ignore time-dependent network dynamics, deriving the joint probability distribution for pre- and postsynaptic degrees and analyzing the resulting random symmetric matrices. We then apply the matrix geometry approach to address the dynamical problem, focusing on the matrix Green function and its connection to joint degree distributions, which enables a systematic analysis of matrix dynamics. We subsequently explore statistical properties, specifically density of states, current fluctuations, and energy dissipation, before concluding that the proposed methodology is applicable to other neural models. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between the random matrix method and mean-field theory. Theta neurons, characterized as excitatory cells that spontaneously oscillate between action potentials and hyperpolarization at frequencies near 7 Hz, are typically analyzed as part of brain rhythm generation mechanisms. However, this work demonstrates that they also constitute a robust framework for analyzing properties of large connected networks. Beyond theoretical analysis, theta neurons are also implemented in spiking neural networks-on-chip to simulate brain activity, providing an avenue for experimental validation of our findings. Additionally, large-scale theta neuron models are used in complex systems to represent spiking neuron networks, making our results relevant to a broad spectrum of neural network applications. Future research may leverage the methods developed here to investigate new neural network structures and designs. a highly effective method for processing graph-structured data by utilizing graph neural message passing for feature aggregation. GNNs have demonstrated success across various graph machine learning applications, including node classification, link prediction, graph classification, and generative modeling. However, GNNs suffer from the over-smoothing problem, where excessive message passing causes node representations to converge to identical values, thereby restricting the model's expressiveness. This work introduces a Graphon Neural Network (GNN*) derived from the graph limit concept of a graph sequence. Specifically, GNN* estimates a graphon from a training graph and generates a continuous function mapping node labels to prediction values. Beyond being theoretically grounded, GNN* offers several practical benefits: (1) it supports transfer learning by predicting graphs within a specific domain; (2) it enhances generalization, particularly for large graphs; and (3) it enables the prediction of graphs with novel node labels. Experimental evaluations confirm that GNN* matches or surpasses the performance of existing GNNs under favorable conditions. Additionally, we observe that GNN* exhibits superior generalization compared to other GNNs when handling graphs significantly larger than those used for training. These findings validate our hypothesis that GNN* mitigates over-smoothing and enhances model performance. The code is accessible at https://github.com/yzh999/GNN. We propose GNN* not only as an alternative to GNNs but also to deepen our understanding of the theoretical boundaries of GNNs. This paper supersedes the version previously accepted by ICLR 2021, addressing several errors and clarifications. The updated code is available at https://github.com/yzh999/GNN. Specifically, the regression loss function has been modified to ensure non-negative values. Please consult the GitHub repository for comprehensive details regarding this update. Furthermore, our code has been incorporated into the ligraph library (https://github.com/Andr019/ligraph). Abstract. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are powerful tools for learning from graph-structured data. However, GNNs suffer from over-smoothing, which significantly hinders their practical performance, prompting a search for novel network architectures to address this limitation. In this paper, we present the Graphon Neural Network (GNN*), a model rooted in graphon theory. Unlike GNNs, GNN* avoids over-smoothing while maintaining competitive performance, validating the critical role of GNN* in mitigating over-smoothing. Index Terms—Graph

This paper introduces a novel concept of utilizing force control alongside an impedance controller—managing the relationship between force and deformation—to execute multi-fingered manipulation. Originally designed to handle updates in streaming environments, CountSketch has seen increasing application within deep learning. This paper introduces a novel application of CountSketch to Bayesian neural networks, where it is employed to approximate the posterior covariance matrix. We model each interaction partner as a generator producing speech signals based on a language model and a modulator adjusting a spectrum shaper using a circular state that tracks the speaker's phonetic spectral bandwidth. This circular state evolves through dynamic balance processes influenced by both the listener and the environment. A learning mechanism is proposed to enable each participant to adapt to the other during interactions, thereby capturing vocal entrainment. Experiments were conducted on two distinct conditions: a lab setting with real human-human interactions and a virtual environment involving human-human simulations. In both cases, both partners gradually adjusted their spectral bandwidths to achieve mutual synchronization. These empirical observations were replicated and explained by the proposed model, demonstrating that both entrainment and disentrainment can emerge depending on the specific context. Ultimately, the parameters of the lab and virtual environments suggest that vocal entrainment likely serves as a cue for establishing social bonds. These findings underscore the need for social robots to learn and replicate vocal entrainment to communicate more naturally and to adapt to various interlocutors by adjusting their spectral bandwidths. This capability allows robots to suggest potential social connections with individuals or groups who exhibit vocal traits similar to their own. Furthermore, spectral bandwidth modulation could act as a social adaptation tool, facilitating interactions across diverse scenarios and partners. These findings also hold significant potential for clinical applications in assisting individuals with social communication disorders, such as autism. Ultimately, spectral bandwidth modulation represents a new dimension of social interaction that social robots should be designed to utilize. In contrast, this paper introduces a more streamlined, modular approach to constructing semantic models for the same calculus. Intrinsic to this method is the distinction between well-typed programs and those with "potential," a concept defined by a subset of the typical typing rules identified as possessing the most descriptive capacity. This proposed technique is both explicit and easy to implement, as it relies on category theory and linear logic proof-nets. It also achieves a degree of modularity by integrating a "qPCF" component, which aligns with the work of Bonchi, Pagani, and Pagani, into the quantum lambda calculus framework. Finally, this paper provides a more detailed comparison of the various semantic methods examined, highlighting the uniqueness of this work, which others have only briefly addressed. As an initial step toward developing a more effective programming language educational model, this research aims to advance the current trajectory of quantum programming language evolution. Additionally, it may assist in forming more robust compositionality within quantum programming, thereby facilitating the creation of more efficient and accurate programs. This study addresses a two-dimensional, time-dependent Stokes system featuring a unilateral constraint that restricts the velocity's negative component in a specific spatial direction. The primary objective is to develop a time-discretization scheme that maintains second-order accuracy in time, alongside a corresponding finite element method ensuring optimal convergence rates, even in the presence of singularities caused by the contact condition. The analysis relies on the mathematical framework of pseudo-monotone operators, a tool widely applicable to various contact problems. The computational scheme is validated through numerical experiments that compare the model's outcomes with a reference solution. The resulting method proves highly effective for solving Stokes systems with unilateral constraints, though it is not exclusive to the Stokes system or the specific nature of the constraint. Instead, it extends to other systems involving Stokes-type pseudo-monotone operators subject to unilateral conditions. The proposed methodology is particularly notable for managing the history effect, as the constraint depends not only on the current time but also on past events. Our numerical investigations confirm that the scheme accurately captures the evolution of this history effect. The structure of the paper is as follows: Section 2 defines the physical model and establishes notations; Section 3 derives an a priori error estimate for the Stokes system with a unilateral condition; Section 4 presents the discretization scheme and demonstrates its second-order temporal accuracy; Section 5 provides numerical examples illustrating the model's capabilities under a unilateral physical condition; and Section 6 presents concluding remarks. Additionally, an appendix outlines several numerical tests of various ice sheet models utilizing a "grounding line" derived from this specific conceptual model and its numerical scheme. These tests highlight how such contact phenomena are prevalent and significant within ice sheet modeling. The findings are also relevant to other physical phenomena in diverse fields, such as the interaction between solid and liquid phases in metallurgy. Finally, the finite element method is derived from a Gamma-convergent approximation of the perimeter functional. Although this work was in progress during the initial lockdown, the conclusion was reached that numerical modeling of physical phenomena was a vital, relevant, and valuable activity. We contend that numerical modeling should be regarded as a fundamental component of a researcher's profile. Our analysis indicates that the proposed finite element method offers reasonable computational costs and delivers results consistent with physical reality. Dust emission in this region is primarily driven by hot interstellar grains heated to temperatures exceeding 30~K by stellar radiation. Our analysis of the dust properties across these areas reveals a gradient in M31's stellar disk: near the nucleus, dust grains are hotter and less porous, exhibiting higher metallicity. Conversely, the outer regions display cooler, more porous grains with lower metallicity. These trends align with similar gradients observed in the Milky Way. Furthermore, M31's dust distribution displays clumpiness at scales ranging from 1000~pc to 10 pc, mirroring trends seen in the Milky Way but distinct from the Spitzer Photometry and Induced Resolved Encensus Survey (SPIRE) observations of M33, which show smoother emission. Additionally, we calculate the dust contribution to the FRB's dispersion measure (DM), showing it accounts for 12% of the total DM. This contribution is consistent with the density and size constraints of the cloud. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where dust contribution to the DM has been directly observed. These findings enhance our understanding of dust's role in the early stages of star and planet formation. Both objects are unusual for their scarcity in molecular gas relative to their mass. We suggest that the difference arises from cloud age, with SN 2011fw cloud being younger than the FRB 20190520 cloud. These discoveries significantly advance our comprehension of cloud evolution and the early phases of star and planet formation. we investigate the connection between initial geometric anisotropies and anisotropic flow within the quark-gluon plasma. While the QMPT model accurately accounts for elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular ($v_3$) flow, it notably underestimates the square of the radial flow coefficient ($k_T$) compared to elliptic and triangular anisotropies. Furthermore, elliptic flow exhibits a stronger correlation with the squared elliptic initial anisotropy ($e_2^2$) than with its magnitude ($e_2$), whereas the triangular anisotropy $e_3$ dominates over its counterpart $5/2 e_{3,5/2}$. In non-central collisions, $v_2$ correlates more strongly with $e_2^2$ than with $e_2$, although $v_2$ shows a weaker dependence on initial geometry than $v_3$. Additionally, $k_T$ demonstrates a significantly weaker dependence on $e_2^2$ compared to $v_2$. These findings indicate an early decoupling of radial flow from the geometric anisotropies of the quark-gluon plasma, consistent with our previous results regarding the evolution of $k_T$ during hadronization. Finally, we observe a distinct decoupling between the elliptic and triangular flow components.

While log analysis is essential for upholding cyber security, traditional approaches are often labor-intensive, time-consuming, and prone to human error. Existing state-of-the-art tools are limited to specific log schemas, such as Log4j or Syslog, rather than handling diverse formats. Furthermore, manual interpretation of current methods fails to automatically identify novel log anomalies, such as brute-force attacks. This study introduces Log2Metric, a log analysis framework that leverages existing unsupervised anomalies to automatically transform logs into metrics and uncover further anomalies by monitoring distributed metrics. By utilizing extensive log statistics, the framework continuously generates domain-specific metrics, including error counts, request volumes, and unique user counts. Based on these metrics, it continuously monitors and dynamically correlates them to detect 11 distinct anomalies, including those causing logistics failures. On average, Log2Metric reduces the detection time for 8 additional anomalies by 3 minutes compared to other methods. The framework enhances the accuracy and coverage of anomaly detection without incurring extra costs. Evaluated on real-world data, Log2Demonstrate successfully transformed 500 million logs into 300 million metrics. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/yzhou520/log2metric. We build a link between the first homology group of a point cloud and the Euler characteristic through the use of persistent homology and specific subcomplexes derived from the point cloud. To perform this analysis, we employ the Delaunay filtration and the minimal convex Delaunay filtration, utilizing the convex hull to define the minimal convex decomposition. We demonstrate several computational applications of these methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The resulting framework not only enhances the interpretation of the Euler characteristic but also establishes a foundation for future applications in machine learning and pattern recognition. The Euler characteristic can be expressed as the difference between the number of components in a point cloud (such as cavities within 3D medical imaging data) and the number of components needed to "fill" these holes. This decomposition enables the utilization of techniques developed for completing persistent homology. Our approach begins by constructing a point cloud representation of a shape using tetrahedra, where each tetrahedron represents a component identified by an algorithm (such as one proposed in [19]) that identifies a characteristic local density. We demonstrate how to apply existing methods for completing persistent homology specifically to these Delaunay filtrations. Finally, we build a feature vector for a point cloud based on its persistence barcode, demonstrating how these constructed features can serve as input for classification models to distinguish between different types of cavities in medical imaging data. The primary objective is to quantify the impact of off-shell and non-resonant effects on the shapes of differential distributions, which are essential for extracting the top quark mass via the template fit method. To achieve this, we conducted a thorough discussion, validated a technique that streamlines the incorporation of arbitrary resummation schemes within a full calculation, and compared various theoretical approaches, including the standard narrow width approximation, a canonical off-shell method, and an approach that integrates soft-gluon resummation to resum logarithms arising from the time ordering of decay events. Our findings indicate that the canonical and NWA approaches yield essentially identical results, while the resummation scheme under development produces divergences in the distributions at next-to-leading logarithmic order relative to the top quark decay width. Additionally, we observed that the soft-gluon emission scheme, which accounts for the phase-space distribution of emitted gluons, can generate biases in the reconstructed invariant mass of the semi-leptonic system that are difficult to interpret as variations in the top quark mass. We also examined the potential for resummation effects to arise at orders beyond next-to-leading logarithmic order, suggesting they could be substantially more significant. In conclusion, our results suggest that to achieve percent-level precision in determining the top quark mass, one must either include the resummation of soft gluons in the hadronic jet's phase space or develop a formalism capable of resummating even virtual corrections. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of missing events due to hadronic leptons falling into jets. Finally, we addressed various aspects of template fitting to directly extract the top quark mass from ttbar production data. We demonstrated that the best fit mass is highly sensitive to the chosen template setup, with variations reaching up to 3 GeV depending on the specific template features. We demonstrated that this strong dependence is largely biased by the model-dependent treatment of jet clustering around the top quark decay products. We propose a method to mitigate this bias, although this remains an open problem. Our recommendations and findings are intended to aid experimental collaborations in designing optimal strategies for top quark mass measurements. We believe these efforts are crucial for achieving a mass precision of approximately 200 MeV in the near future, a level of accuracy that is also of significant value for testing the Standard Model. To address these challenges, training in real-world settings is impractical; instead, high-fidelity simulators serve as essential proxies. This paper introduces a novel framework that enables the training of RL agents on such simulators and their seamless transfer to vehicles. Our approach employs a highly flexible method for constructing simulators from existing, potentially heterogeneous, driving simulations. Through ablation studies and benchmark evaluations using the open-source CARLA simulator, we demonstrate that our framework effectively facilitates simulation-to-reality transfer and offers viable solutions to the high cost and safety concerns associated with RL training in these environments. to enhance the efficiency of evolutionary computation. Typically, the optimization task is treated as a single task, with measures such as runtime or energy consumption as optimization goals. However, in real-world scenarios, tasks often exhibit diverse quality dimensions. This study introduces multiple measure multi-task optimization (MMTO), a method designed to optimize various quality aspects simultaneously. Because directly applying existing multi-objective optimization techniques is not straightforward in this context, we propose a parallel evolutionary approach. Additionally, to harness the benefits of modern multi- and many-core architectures, we develop a multi-processor framework that executes the proposed algorithm in parallel. We evaluated MMTO and its parallel implementation across three synthetic tasks and two real-world energy efficiency cases. The results demonstrate that MMTO can effectively address multi-measure issues within evolutionary algorithms, and its parallel implementation successfully exploits modern multi-processor architectures to deliver multi-measure optimized outcomes. Furthermore, our implementation achieves superior efficiency compared to other known IMPO methods when applied to real-world tasks. Finally, we provide an analysis of the performance characteristics of this multi-measure multi-task algorithm (3M2) on specific hardware architectures. Our goal is for this research to guide the design of future multi-measure multi-task algorithms and their implementation on modern multi-processor systems. 17-BLG-1430 was recently confirmed as a binary star system hosting an Earth-mass exoplanet orbiting at approximately 0.3 AU. This study investigates the gravitational effects of such a planetary system on light rays that graze the Sun during the microlensing alignment. We demonstrate that while a well-separated planetary system can be identified during the primary eclipse using the caustic structure, it remains undetectable during the secondary eclipse. Our predictions for the microlensing light curve, specifically regarding the secondary eclipse, should be validated against the OGLE database. While noise could obscure the planar caustic, the absence of clear noise in OGLE's monitoring of this event enables a search for the companion. Although there is a non-zero probability of missing the planet due to noise, this does not significantly alter the inferred mass of the planetary system. Furthermore, we show that the additional noise does not affect the mass determination of the host star. This research extends the application of caustic studies from exoplanetary systems to planet-sized objects, and by applying this method to Sun-grazing events, it paves the way for the first direct detection of planets orbiting our Sun. The current search represents a pioneering effort in exploring the Solar System through microlensing. Future observations by the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope are expected to increase the number of suitable events, thereby facilitating the study of planets within our own solar system. The identification of the companion in the first such discovered event will naturally stimulate a broader search among other events, with the anticipation of revealing the architecture of a well-studied planetary system. Additionally, we show that this methodology can be extended to provide constraints on the existence of the Moon by analyzing light curves from microlensing events that graze the Sun. However, when resonance occurs between the fundamental driving frequency andFloquet sidebands—specifically when driving amplitude dependence is significant—these established methods fail. This paper examines this specific resonance condition using a one-dimensional dimer chain model charged with a high-harmonic electric field. Through numerical analysis, we demonstrate that the system exhibits duality between topological insulating and metallic phases during a slow time-periodic drive, resulting in resonant enhancements of transition rates from the topological insulator phase to the metallic phase. Our findings hold specific relevance for research into topological insulators and quantum spin liquids subjected to high harmonic loading. Our study provides a systematic and comprehensive understanding of new, previously unobserved physical phenomena, facilitating further investigations into Floquet engineering. At ambient pressure, the low-temperature ferromagnetic fluctuations in this heavy-fermion system are known to be extremely weak, facilitating the proximity of a $d$-wave superconductor to a quantum critical point. Our data indicate that long-range order vanishes at approximately 0.1 GPa, after which the magnetic susceptibility remains a power law down to the superconducting transition temperature, which subsequently shifts to a minimum near 2 GPa before rising again. These findings underscore the sensitivity of superconductivity to low-energy magnetic excitations and provide evidence that superconducting fluctuations coexist with a magnetically disordered state in CeCoIn5. Furthermore, since hydrostatic pressure effectively tunes the hybridization between conduction electrons and 4$f$ electrons, these results confirm that long-range order is absent in all heavy-fermion systems exhibiting superconductivity near a magnetic quantum critical point.

(HI) maps, covering extensive areas, are vital for advancing our understanding of galaxy evolution, structure, and content. While various galactic disks have been studied for decades, such sensitive and resolved maps are currently available for only a few external galaxies. This paper introduces a new HI map of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) based on observations from the Arecibo HI Survey of Magellanic Clouds (AHSM). The map spans 680 deg² with 7 arcmin resolution and achieves a 1-mJy beam⁻¹ sensitivity (3σ), covering 1654 beams across a velocity range of ± ±200 km s⁻¹. The total HI mass is measured at 6.5 ± 0.3 × 10⁸ M⊙ within a ± ±100 km s⁻¹ velocity window. Inside ± ±200 km s⁻¹, the map detects 8.6 ± 0.3 × 10⁸ M⊙, which accounts for 37% of the map's 2.31 ± 0.06 × 10⁸ M⊙. Beyond the known HII regions, HI rings, and the HI ring associated with 30 Doradus, the remaining excess emission (3.1 ± 0.3 × 10⁸ M⊙) is likely due to absorption from the SMC's extended HI disk, which falls below the map's sensitivity floor. The distribution of HI rings and the newly identified HI clouds in this map align with the central stellar bar and 30 Doradus. The cloud located SWW of the bar matches the position of the Magellanic Bridge, while three clouds located NEE likely originate from material stripped by tidal forces during the formation of the Leading Magellanic Stream. The map also resolves previously unresolved HI clouds, such as those surrounding the star-forming regions W31C and N132B, as well as those surrounding LMC bars and rings. Additionally, it identifies new clouds near W49, N48, and 30 Doradus, with a tentative detection near 30 Doradus A. This map will facilitate a more detailed analysis of the SMC's HI structure and its interaction with the SMC, LMC, SMC-1, LMC-1, and the Leading Magellanic Stream

proven highly effective for node classification, existing approaches for multi-label multigraph classification suffer from two primary limitations. First, they typically treat all edge types uniformly when aggregating neighbor information, neglecting the distinct roles played by different edge types in representing a node's community structure. Second, they fail to leverage the inherent complementarity among multiple label sets during the multi-label prediction process. To address these issues, we introduce the Dual Local-Global Attentional GNN (DLGA-GNN). First, to capitalize on the relationships between label sets, we design an inductive multi-head multi-label self-attention module. This module learns independent and uncorrelated local attentional embeddings for each label set and fuses them into a global attentional embedding, thereby improving the quality of the learned gnode label embedding. Second, to exploit the interrelationships among different neighbors of a gnode, we propose learning separate local self-attentional embeddings for each neighbor and aggregating them based on label set compatibility. Finally, to ensure sufficient model capacity, we project features back to the input space after self-attention feature aggregation. Extensive experiments confirm that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. 9-4842.1, located at approximately 100 Mpc, is classified as a double LIRAC galaxy and serves as a rare example of a LIRAC galaxy pair. This system is notable for being the first case where both galaxies exhibit a double-peak CO spectrum. We present new observations of the system's CO(1-0) spectrum, alongside observations of CO(2-1), CO(3-2), and an extensive survey of CO(6-5), which yielded only one detection. Additionally, we report a new HST/NICMOS observation at 1.6 μm, which reveals a double-peak flux distribution. Based on these findings, we calculate the system's luminosity and flux for the CO(6-5) transition as well as for the HST/NICMOS band. We utilize standard assumptions to estimate stellar mass, SFR, and HST/NICMOS flux, and we employ the "2D deconvolution" method to derive the system's position angle, ellipticity, and axis ratio. Finally, we compare our results with existing literature and conduct a physical analysis of the system. Our physical analysis indicates that the system is likely in a merger phase, with notable asymmetry between the two LIRAC galaxies. Specifically, the differences in their CO(6-5) flux suggest variations in stellar age. This study contributes to the understanding of LIRAC galaxies as key components in galaxy evolution. RXCJ0232.9-4842.1 is the first LIRAC galaxy pair with precisely determined position angles, allowing for direct comparison with nearby CO observations. Furthermore, this work represents the first detection of CO(6-5) emission from a galaxy at this redshift. These observations are part of a project that also secured a CO(6-5) detection from the galaxy SDSS J0942+11306. This detection is significant because it provides direct evidence of the presence of a molecular torus. We also observe that CO(6-5) flux is generally lower in starburst galaxies compared to LIRAGs or UDGs, supporting the hypothesis that such galaxies possess a molecular torus. This report presents recommendations arising from an invited workshop on the scientific, technical, and financial aspects of establishing a proton accelerator to support an electron-positron collider near the International Linear Collider Site at CEBAF Near 200 (CLIC Near 200). Finally, the working group will assess various options for powering the collider with existing grid electricity versus a dedicated accelerator power plant. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) offers a strategy to directly discover deep network configurations from hyperparameter space, often outperforming manually designed or evolutionarily tuned architectures. This paper introduces a novel method, "Neural Architecture Search for Reinforcement Learning" (NAS4RL), which facilitates the automatic and simultaneous search for both deep network architectures and their learning parameters. Specifically, we employ Normalized Susceptibility Sampling (NSS) to perform reinforcement learning-based searches within the architectural space. To represent architectural details, we utilize vectors encoding features like activation functions, normalization methods, and dropout rates. We also introduce an activation function lookup layer (AFL) to enhance the expressiveness of the search space, enabling the agent to determine not only the activation type but also its hyperparameters. Experiments on standard deep learning benchmarks—MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100—demonstrate that incorporating NSS and AFL allows NAS4RL to rapidly identify network architectures that surpass those designed by experts. Furthermore, when evaluating the learned architectures and training parameters on these same benchmarks, our approach yields performance improvements. To our knowledge, this is the first work to simultaneously optimize both network architecture and training parameters via a unified network structure. This study presents the findings from a series of runs utilizing $^{12}$C-embedded scintillating crystals, executed between 2012 and 2017 at CEA-Grenoble. Notably, the 2014 and 2016 runs employed a double-crystal configuration weighing 388 grams, shielded by 2 meters of lead and situated 1 meter beneath the Earth's surface. Analysis of nuclear recoil data yielded a sensitivity to the nuclear scattering cross section of $7.8^{+0.9}_{-0.7} \times 10^{-41}$ cm$^2$/nucleon at an energy transfer of 4.5 keV. A subsequent re-examination of these results, incorporating a more comprehensive set of background events, refined this sensitivity to $1.9 \times 10^{-40}$ cm$^2$/nucleon at 4.5 keV, aligning with the previously established 90% confidence level limit for weakly interacting sub-GeV particles and significantly enhancing the constraints on WIMPs. The current dataset exhibits a sensitivity extending to scattering cross sections near $10^{-36}$ cm$^2$ (at 15 keV$_{nr}$), thereby opening a novel window into the search for dark matter. Furthermore, these results provide valuable insights into the detection capabilities of CRESST for the upcoming experiment, CRESST-III. Given the experiment's existing infrastructure and historical data, the potential to identify dark matter signals within the existing dataset should be investigated. Additionally, these efforts contribute to establishing stricter constraints on "WIMP millicules," a scenario proposing the existence of dark matter composed of multiple distinct particle species. Contemporary consensus algorithms are frequently engineered to optimize performance under favorable conditions, yet many deploy inefficient fallback mechanisms when these optimal conditions are not met. For example, when sufficient honest nodes are not immediately accessible within the initial communication rounds, certain algorithms may require nearly cubic communication complexity to reach a decision. This paper presents the first distributed consensus solution that guarantees a constant number of communication rounds for the majority of honest nodes, regardless of the specific environment. Unlike existing algorithms, this solution eliminates unnecessary rings or expensive fallback mechanisms. We validate the solution's efficiency through implementation and experimentation, demonstrating that it achieves nearly an order-of-magnitude improvement over widely adopted alternatives like PBFT and Hotstuff. Furthermore, we benchmark it against cutting-edge solutions, showing it matches their performance while offering a significant advantage in more common scenarios. Consensus is a critical requirement for distributed systems, yet its design has often been constrained by theoretical limitations; this paper demonstrates how incorporating practical insights can yield superior performance. By allowing environmental assumptions, our solution surpasses the constant-round benchmarks established by theory-based algorithms like Tura and Corbert et al. Additionally, theory often favors algorithms with high communication complexity to verify decisions in adverse scenarios; however, our approach reveals that these complexities are frequently unnecessary for honest nodes in the typical use cases where the majority of nodes are honest. Our approach maintains constant rounds for over 66% of honest nodes without relying on slow or costly fallback mechanisms, achieving this constant-round guarantee across all scenarios through efficient probabilistic methods. This work is the outcome of over two years of research and implementation. Consensus remains a persistent challenge for distributed systems, hindering widespread adoption in practical scenarios. Consensus protocols are increasingly utilized across diverse domains, including cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, as well as enterprise environments in finance, cloud computing, and databases. We examine how the specific requirements of these domains influence the selection of consensus algorithms and present a survey of protocols used in these environments, offering guidelines for choosing an appropriate algorithm based on specific constraints. For instance, we identify that protocols with high communication complexity are rarely necessary given the typical ratio of honest nodes. By leveraging these practical insights, we have developed protocols outperforming those designed primarily by theoretical computer scientists. Consensus protocols are continuously evolving, and we outline key future research directions to help theorists create the next generation of consensus algorithms. The most promising opportunity lies in applying our methodology to design protocols that ensure a constant number of rings for all honest nodes. This could involve increasing randomness to minimize rings

The resulting modified Friedmann equation retains the same structure as the APS LQC model; however, the critical matter density required for the bounce is half that of the original Loop Quantum Cosmology (LQC) framework. This reduction in the critical density arises because the simplified commutation relation for holonomies of the time-rotation connection, K, yields half the number of non-zero zero-modes compared to those for holonomies of the spatial-connection A in the APS model. Since the number of non-zero zero-modes directly influences the minimal area-volume, this difference accounts for the variation in the critical density. Consequently, both the area- and volume-operator in the proposed model exhibit LQC-type modified eigenvalue spectra, yet the maximum eigenvalue for the area-operator is half that of the APS LQC model. This discrepancy is attributed to the absence of a zero-mode for the holonomy of the SU(1,1) K-connection along a simple closed loop within the spatially-sliced phase space. Furthermore, this analysis demonstrates that the semiclassical quantum state remains a viable method for detecting LQC phenomena in cosmological models. Finally, we suggest that both the novel ADM-based LQC and the Ashtekar-Ashtekar-Vilenkin (AVW) model are applicable to more general cosmological scenarios. This conclusion is supported by numerical results indicating that the semiclassical quantum state to probe LQC in a general cosmological context is also capable of revealing LQC effects. In summary, this study provides an alternative derivation of a Loop Quantum Cosmological model distinct from the standard literature, utilizes a different connection variable, and offers an alternative pathway to modified eigenvalue spectra for the area-volume operator. Additionally, it establishes a more rigorous theoretical foundation for choosing the argument of the sine function for holonomies of K to derive the correct area-volume modified eigenvalue spectrum. The differences between the models in the new and old LQC literature may have significant implications for the quantum state description and the detection of LQC phenomena. This work also holds potential for extending the study of LQC models to more general scenarios. Finally, it is noted that the numerical analysis in this paper complements the recent work by Chen et al. (2022), which employed the old LQC model to investigate the large-scale structure of the universe. In contrast, the new LQC model presented here could contribute to cosmological studies beyond simple inflationary models. In

This challenge is especially critical in scenarios involving hidden Markov model neural network learning (HMNN), where the count of discrete states used as Bayesian decision boundaries must be selected a priori. HMNNs extend deterministic neural networks by incorporating stochastic state transitions and outputs, offering a principled approach to learning uncertainty within data, transitions, and predictions. The proposed method employs a two-phase strategy. Initially, an incremental neural network is trained on data features to identify the optimal number of discrete states a priori by analyzing continuous state-transition density heatmaps. Subsequently, an uncertainty metric, realized as a categorical output distribution, is trained based on instantaneous state-transition probabilities to facilitate Bayesian decision-making. The study validates this approach across diverse robotics tasks, yielding successful state estimations with notable prediction accuracy under uncertainty. Specifically, experiments on an underwater robotic vehicle demonstrate that predictive uncertainty enhances decision accuracy in noisy environments by 12% to 33% compared to analogous deep neural network methods. Furthermore, uncertainty measures aid in enhancing downstream tasks such as image classification and object detection. These findings underscore that uncertainty-aware learning serves as a vital component for developing reliable, high-performance autonomous robotic systems capable of making informed decisions even with imperfect information. This paper addresses the data scarcity issue by introducing a novel generative adversarial network (GAN) architecture and architectural design to improve traffic flow prediction. Specifically, we propose the Traffic-GAN model, which integrates an auxiliary generative network designed to produce realistic traffic patterns. Within medical science specific to disease progression, a particularly significant achievement is the development of the first cell-type transition map for Alzheimer's disease. This model successfully predicted cell fate during experimental conditions, demonstrating profound implications for understanding disease mechanisms and driving cell-based therapies. This study aims to establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for cell fate maps by applying the-same- concept pioneered in biological gene regulation networks and model-theoretic modal logic. We achieve this by employing the Confluence of Rewriting Systems, with a particular emphasis on Non-Confluent Strategies, to elucidate how specific transition maps function while managing exceptions. Specifically, a Rewriting System is utilized to represent a transition map, and the associativity of the associated rewrite relation defines the process of cell fate progression. Building on this, exception handling is framed as a conflict resolution mechanism, where the concept of confluence assists in defining mathematical properties that ensure the robustness of the transition maps. Consequently, this research deepens the connection between mathematical rewriting theory and cell fate maps and holds potential applicability for various other cell-based processes. Furthermore, these findings offer a fresh conceptual approach to rewriting theory, particularly regarding the non-confluent resolution of exceptions. While deep learning is the prevailing method, it typically demands extensive training on a specific dataset, leading models to rely on idiosyncratic features. This results in poor generalization when encountering new data with distinct characteristics, such as those from different hospitals. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel GAN-based framework called DLF-GAN. This system learns hippocampus segmentation by incorporating detailed anatomical relationships from an incomplete hippocampal atlas. The model comprises a segmentation network (SegNet) and a discriminator (DiscNet). SegNet is trained to produce accurate hippocampus masks, while DiscNet attempts to confuse the segmentation outputs with the ground truth anatomical relationships. This adversarial process continues until SegNet becomes robust enough to deceive DiscNet. Compared to standard deep learning approaches, DLF-GAN delivers superior performance on both in-domain and cross-domain segmentation tasks. Experimental results indicate that the model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in hippocampus segmentation. Furthermore, the t-SNE visualization of SegNet's final layer demonstrates that the model has successfully learned fine-grained anatomical connections between hippocampus sub-regions. Using weak values, we expose the internal inconsistency of this description. By introducing transversal modes, we detect emerging correlations between path and traversal degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we analyze the rotational symmetry of the output pattern as an indicator of pairwise interactions, finding no obvious connection between this symmetry and the probability of detecting three particles in a single output. Finally, we outline modifications to the experimental setup proposed to investigate the quantum pigeonhole effect in a more straightforward manner. We recommend experimental efforts to either observe or explain strong particle-pair correlations in the transversal modes, even at high rotational symmetry, as a means to achieve a consistent understanding of the phenomenon. These observations could, for the first time, deeply clarify the underlying physics of quantum interference. Such insights could significantly advance the practical application of interferometric arrangements that challenge classical intuition, including those utilized in multi-party quantum secret sharing protocols. The proposed modifications may prove valuable for exploring the fundamental limits of these protocols. Furthermore, this study underscores the potential of quantum optical experiments using single sources to address foundational questions in quantum mechanics, even when the particle count exceeds the scale typically considered large. This capacity to investigate quantum phenomena through relatively large numbers of particles may offer an alternative approach for testing quantum theory in scenarios where macroscopic superpositions pose technical difficulties. Such considerations may also provide preliminary groundwork for proposed quantum gravity experiments. Additionally, these experiments could prepare the groundwork for larger-scale tests of quantum mechanics through multi-party quantum secret sharing. A successful explanation or observation of strong particle-pair correlations could pave the way for enhancing security in quantum secret sharing protocols. Current efforts should focus on clarifying the physical reality within the established experimental framework. By adopting a pragmatic approach, we can simultaneously advance both theoretical and practical understanding of the experiment. We believe this strategy offers a more effective means of gaining a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon than pursuing speculative extensions of the experiment. While FL enhances data privacy by retaining user information locally, it remains susceptible to privacy breaches through model inversion and membership inference attacks. To mitigate these risks, we apply Differential Privacy noise to gradient updates within FL algorithms. Drawing inspiration from this mechanism, we develop a hybrid approach combining Graph Neural Networks (GNN) with Differential Privacy noise, termed FL-DP-GNN. We assess this method against existing state-of-the-art techniques using standard evaluation metrics. Our evaluation examines both global model training scenarios and FL implementations, addressing membership inference and isolation attacks on both user and server sides. Experimental results demonstrate that FL-DP-GNN achieves superior performance in maintaining privacy compared to other state-of-the-art methods. These findings confirm that FL-DP-GNN delivers high recommendation accuracy while significantly minimizing the risk of privacy leakage. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first study to apply FL combined with Differential Privacy to graph-based recommendation models. $G = (V, E)$ where two players, Alice and Bob, take turns selecting a vertex $w$ in each move. Initially, Alice picks $w_0$, after which Bob selects $w_1$ subject to the constraint that $w_1$ must be non-adjacent to $w_0$. The game proceeds with both players alternating turns, starting from $w_0$. Alice wins if she can choose a sequence such that every vertex in $G$ is selected either by her or blocks a vertex she has already chosen; specifically, any remaining unchosen vertices must form an independent set. The minimum number of moves required for Alice to guarantee a win is termed her winning number. The objective of this study is to provide upper and lower bounds for this number. We demonstrate that these quantities are closely linked to the minimum size of a dominating set in the open neighborhood of any vertex (known as a semidominating set), alongside the order and maximum degree of the graph. Additionally, we analyze various graph classes to establish the exact winning number for $C_4$, a specific subset of bipartite graphs, and to determine lower bounds for $C_{2k+1}$ ($k \geq 2$), $C_6$, and all bipartite graphs. Traditionally, the abstract fixpoint is derived by successively applying a monotonic semantic function $F : \mathbb{A} \to \mathbb{A}$ to an initial approximation $\mathsf{seed} \in \mathbb{A}$, continuing until $F(\mathsf{result}) = \mathsf{result}$. This paper introduces a refined approach where certain iterations are delegated to a black-box procedure capable of approximating $F$'s fixpoint. We demonstrate the utility of this method in TAPA, a traditional, declarative tool for abstract interpretation. TAPA comes with a language where a formalization of $F$ and $\mathsf{seed}$ defines a program's abstract semantics. We enhance this formalization to allow user specifications where a portion of $F$ is replaced by a black-box procedure. This modification yields a novel tool capable of leveraging existing or future black-box techniques, thereby expanding the range of applicable abstract interpretations. This work is, in part, based on the paper "Abstract Interpretation Revisited" by the authors, which was recognized as a best paper at APLAS 2021. Additionally, the updated tool TAPA has been incorporated into the MOPSY research group's existing abstract interpretation framework. The framework, along with the new black-box supported feature, is now available at https://www.mopsy.de/tapa/. Furthermore, the source code for the framework and tool has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/mopsy/TAPA. These resources, including the updated version of the tool, can be utilized for further research in abstract interpretation, such as exploring black-box based approaches. The updated version of the paper "Abstract Interpretation Revisited" by the authors acknowledges this black-box enhancement. This work also builds upon the paper "TAPA: Interactive Abstract Interpretation," by the authors, which was accepted as a long paper at ICSE 2021. That publication introduced an interactive language and tool for abstract interpretation, enabling users to define the seed and abstract semantics of a program's interpretation while viewing and editing the resulting fixpoint at any stage of the computation. This study employs magnetic pressure to destabilize the low-spin magnetic structure of the semiconducting oxide MnSiO₃, inducing spin-crossover (SCO) to a high-spin state. Using density functional theory, we identify two local minima corresponding to these distinct spin configurations and calculate how various perovskite layers—whether magnetic or non-magnetic, ideal or distorted—alter lattice parameters, bond angles, and interlayer distances to facilitate or hinder SCO. Among the examined perovstrite compounds, MnSiO₃ exhibits one of the strongest correlations between structural geometry and SCO. Extensive first-principles analysis reveals that high-spin SCO is accompanied by a significant increase in the in-plane M-O bond, whereas SCO does not necessarily result in a perovskite structure flattening. Furthermore, MnSiO₃ demonstrates an exceptional expansion in the interlayer distance, driven by the specific interaction between the high-spin MnO₆ octahedra and SiO₂ tetrahedra. Ultimately, MnSiO₃ emerges as an exceptional case where structural distortations are intrinsically linked to SCO through geometric frustration arising between high-spin MnO₆ octahedra and SiO₂ tetrahedra. These findings underscore the critical role of interlayer interactions facilitated by specific geometrical arrangements in driving SCO. Consequently, MnSiO₃ serves as an ideal system for investigating the structure-property relationships of SCO phenomena. Additionally, this work paves the way for designing new perovskites with tailored magnetic structures and robust SCO behaviors. Finally, we demonstrate that SCO induces substantial changes in optical properties, suggesting potential applications in optomagnetic devices utilizing tunable oxide perovskites. Furthermore, we predict that SCO induces significant changes in thermal conductivity, opening a new avenue for developing tunable thermoelectric materials. Overall, our findings provide fundamental insights into the structure-property relationships governing SCO phenomena within perovskite systems. Furthermore, these results enable the exploration of new perovskites featuring large SCO amplitudes and exceptional geometrical distortations. These findings generalize our previous scalar model results—where a scalar variable represented the electromagnetic field amplitude and simple forces acted upon it—to a realistic 3D atom coupled to the full quantum electromagnetic field. Additionally, we provide an explicit operator-level generalization of the scalar model. As expected, the presence of the mirror modifies the transition and radiation rates compared to free space; however, for a mirror at large distances, scalar and quantum electrodynamics yield identical effects, and the mirror's influence diminishes according to an inverse square law with its separation. Furthermore, atomic polarizability introduces a time-asymmetry into the rate equations, creating an apparent violation of detailed balance when the Miror is distant. We explain this apparent contradiction by demonstrating that a specific component of the photon flux from the mirror to the atom must be accounted for. These analytical findings are supported by numerical evidence. Our methodology is rigorous, exact, and fully quantized, yet remains sufficiently simple to facilitate explicit calculations of transition rates, polaryzability effects, and photon emission rates. We anticipate that these techniques and results will find applications across various regimes of atom-light interactions. We also suggest their utility in analyzing models featuring non-linear atom-light couplings and in informing the understanding of similar models within high-temperature or highly relativistic regimes. Finally, we propose these approaches are suitable for resolving the paradox arising from Unruh radiation in accelerating atom models. Specifically, we propose an experimental verification to demonstrate that, consistent with the thermal equilibrium of a system in acceleration, excitation and de-excitation rates balance each other. Our approach emphasizes numerical simplicity, allowing experimentalists to determine feasibility without prior calculation. These remarks are motivated by recent progress in atom trapping and manipulation. We anticipate these proposals and discussions will assist experimentalists in designing appropriate experimental programs. We also propose specific experimental metrics to quantitatively evaluate progress in these efforts. We believe this approach will enable a timely assessment of the success of such initiatives. We hope this will encourage further experimental work to experimentally confirm that no similar thermodynamic paradoxes exist. A primary approach involves constructing mathematical or numerical models to bridge the gap between simple primitive models and complex real-world systems; however, these intermediate models often remain too intricate for direct efficient simulation. The present study investigates a method for simulating specific numerical models that include a particular numerical parameter across a continuous range. We introduce and evaluate various simulation strategies, introducing the concept of a strategy curve and establishing criteria for selecting an optimal curve. As an application, we employ this framework to simulate a numerical model featuring a continuous parameter. Given that many modern scientific models are highly complex and involve multiple parameters, we extend this approach to a multidimensional setting and apply it to a case study of a complex real-world problem. This case study Simulates a computational model of a Japanese forest affected by the Great East Japan Earthquake, utilizing parameters derived from various empirical models and observations. In NSLMXBs, type-C QPOs appear during the transition between thermal and non-thermal accretion flow regimes, suggesting that magnetic fields play a crucial role in accretion disk physics. This important finding has not yet been replicated in magnetars. We report a new type-C event from 4U 0142+069, a well-known magnetar. The event's properties align with those seen in NSLMXBXs, supporting the idea that type-C QPOs offer a unique method for identifying magnetars in X-ray surveys. Furthermore, the detection of this event in 4U 0142+069 provides additional evidence for the unique role of magnetic fields in disk physics and a potential explanation for why only a few type-C events have been observed across the entire population. In the latter part of the study, we explore the potential for using type-C events in X-ray timing to constrain the equation of state for neutron stars. We find that if the type-C event in 4U 0142+069 originates from the same emission mechanism as in NSLMXBs, it implies a maximum radius of 28 km for 1.4 solar mass neutron stars, based on current state-of-the-art equations of state. Additionally, assuming the type-C event results from resonant interaction between the fundamental $l=2$ oscillation mode of the accretion disk and the fundamental radial ($l=0$) oscillation mode of the neutron star, we determine a typical gravitational radius of 11.8 km and a typical spin period of 2.8 s for magnetars. These proposed mechanisms agree with previously reported timing results. Our findings suggest that future type-C events should be utilized to better understand neutron star properties. In the upcoming section, we will discuss new timing results for X0327+365, a previously reported type-C event. We will also investigate whether energy-dependent spectral variations can explain the observed energy dependence of type-C events. We introduce an exact, non-iterative pricing formula that ensures the Nash equilibrium within this competition corresponds to the solution of a convex optimization problem. This approach serves as a precise alternative to previously proposed approximate formulas, particularly in scenarios involving small demand relative to supply capacity, where it provides insightful guidance on system design from a consumer perspective. Their study utilized simulated clusters to investigate whether high-resolution X-ray imaging would reveal numerous small-scale arc-like features caused by shocks and turbulence. The authors found that in simulated Abell class clusters, numerous small-scale structures, filamentary patterns, and bubbles would indeed be visible in high-resolution X-ray tomographic reconstructions, aligning closely with observational data from the Perseus and Whipple clusters. This finding helps explain the scarcity of existing low-resolution X-ray images, which lack the detailed features described by Meneghetti et al. Despite the study confirming that future telescopes will uncover more complex intracluster structures, the authors failed to explicitly address why most low-resolution images do not show these features, thereby missing a critical opportunity to clarify historical discrepancies. Furthermore, they did not fully explore the potential for utilizing higher-resolution imaging to gain deeper insights into the intracluster medium. Finally, the study did not critically evaluate the validity of using simulated clusters to model real astronomical objects for the purpose of understanding their actual dynamics. Collectively, these omissions represent a significant missed chance to provide meaningful new contributions to the field. Ultimately, this work serves as a cautionary example of the risks inherent in relying on simulated clusters to represent real astronomical phenomena. Such an approach is especially problematic for simulating clusters, as their inherent complexity and diversity make them difficult to model accurately. Additionally, the internal complexity of the intracluster medium and its interaction with surrounding factors pose substantial challenges for these simulations. Ultimately, the study highlights the need for more rigorous methods in simulating both galaxy clusters and their internal dynamics. Without such distinctions, we risk perpetuating ungrounded assumptions and potentially invalid conclusions. Ultimately, addressing these discrepancies is essential for the continued validity and progress of astronomical research. acoustic systems characterized by spatially complex, exponential-scale eigenfunctions. We introduce a data-driven method that utilizes these eigenfunctions to construct a low-rank representation of the physics-governing PDEs in the spatial coordinates. By projecting the original high-dimensional system onto the spatial basis derived from the eigenfunctions, we achieve model-order reduction to a full-order linear time-invariant system, which is subsequently approximated as a low-order system using the singular value decomposition-based proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) method. Although the POD-based approach is computationally efficient, it may fail to capture critical system dynamics if the POD-truncated parts contain essential information. Leveraging the low-rank nature of the governing equations, we propose a novel reduced-order model based on a kernel-based extension of the POD method, which retains discarded dynamics by embedding them within the POD subspace. The efficacy and accuracy of both standard POD and the proposed kernel-based models are evaluated across two acoustic parametric cases. Furthermore, a kernel regularization term is incorporated to address the overfitting issue, enhancing the robustness of the model across a broad range of inputs. Finally, a time series forecasting framework is developed for the acoustic reduced-order model to predict unknown outputs from available data. The forecasting accuracy of the kernel-based reduced-order model is compared against a Gaussian process-based approach to demonstrate the proposed model's effectiveness. A key benefit of the kernel-based reduced-order model regarding forecasting is that the proper modes identified through the low-rank property of the PDEs are explicitly integrated into the forecasting algorithm. Additionally, a k-nearest neighbor-based approach is employed to estimate hyper-parameters for optimal forecasting performance. The proposed algorithm's accuracy is assessed using both synthetic and real-world datasets. These results confirm that the kernel-based reduced-order model outperforms the POD-based one in both reduced system modeling and time series forecasting. This work represents a significant advancement in accurately and efficiently reducing the order of acoustic reduced systems. In this mechanism, advertisers and publishers participate in simultaneous online auctions to determine both the price and the allocation of advertising space. Specifically, both parties submit bids to the exchange: the publisher seeks to sell the space, while the advertiser aims to purchase it. Our model assigns a fraud score to each ad request; when a fraud detector identifies a request as fraudulent, it notifies participating exchanges, and the exchange subsequently denies the request. of non-classicality in continuous-variable quantum systems. This study explores their interplay within the framework of conditional systems, a specific subset of bipartitional structures. We demonstrate that if one component of such a system violates Leggett-Garg inequalities conditionally, then the entire structure exhibits Wigner negativity. This finding leverages a recently developed connection between Wigner negativity and Leggett-Garg inequalities. Additionally, we establish that Wigner negativity can be extracted through distillation processes that maintain consistency with the non-locality distillation framework. Finally, we investigate the distillation of Leggett-Garg nonlocality conditional systems, proving that distilling Wigner negativity involves distilling at least one conditional system from the original structure. These results open a new pathway for investigating the relationship between these two non-classicality measures. Our approach relies on operational properties, specifically distillation processes that are robust across various contexts. Beyond their independent significance for conditional quantum systems, these findings offer a fresh perspective on how Wigner negativity and Leggett-Garg nonlocality intersect. Specifically, we address the previously unclear issue of whether the absence of Wigner negativity in a conditional system implies the absence of quantum correlations. By utilizing distillation processes that are universally robust for both context-independent and context-dependent scenarios, we construct criteria for distinguishing between these two cases. This paper introduces a novel class of CPM formats optimized for non-coherent detection that are less sensitive to channel phase variations and Doppler shifts, thereby enhancing robustness in multipath environments. Finally, we observe that the proposed all-one non-coherent detector is not limited to all-one CPM formats but can be extended to general CPM formats. Additionally, we find that for practical applications, a modulation index of 0.5 is more appropriate for achieving optimal performance. These findings are also applicable to coherent detection. In summary, our scheme offers either a more robust non-coherent detector for a specific format or a higher performance detector for a given complexity in terms of phase shifts. Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, yet most current approaches to shaped learning rely on expensive, item-by-item human feedback for individual comparisons. Significant efforts have been made to develop efficient comparators that reduce learning time; however, we argue that human effort can be equally costly. To address this, we investigate methods to boost the efficiency of human effort during interactive labeling by exploiting high-level abstractions. We investigate and develop visual guidance and elite states as effective abstractions. Specifically, we apply dimensionality reduction and visualization to visualize the state space, enabling users to label comparisons on a plot to influence the entire policy. We also identify that feedback on elite states is effective at guiding policies, and we develop an efficient method to elicit this feedback. Experiments show that both visual guidance and elite states significantly outperform random feedback, drastically reducing shaped learning time. Furthermore, we establish that efforts in both cases can be nearly as efficient as those for manually shaped RL v2 comparisons. Finally, we demonstrate through ablation studies and visualization examples that this guidance does not alter policy semantics, indicating that the guidance merely accelerates learning without changing the underlying approach. This work paves the way for humans to effectively shape policies in RL tasks.

The spin angular momentum contributes a constant $+q\hbar/\abs{e}$. At extreme energies, the total angular momentum approaches $n^2(q\hbar/e)$. Consequently, each large extension of the magnetic field's quantum vacuum angular momentum generates two gravitational waves; for the $n$th extension, this occurs twice per period with a power scaling as $n^4$. This suggests a potential means to test the time variation of electromagnetic coupling and the scale of virtual electromagnetic vacuum. This rule suggests a new source of angular momentum for black holes, potentially explaining unobserved gravitational waves from binary black holes, a mechanism for extracting energy from rotating black holes, and a potential explanation for the magnetic field within a hadron. However, this assumption fails in dynamic multi-agent settings, particularly when dealing with non-stationary targets. In such scenarios, equilibrium learning algorithms often struggle to converge or become susceptible to adversarial attacks. This paper introduces a novel, mathematically rigorous framework for learning under non-stationarity, defining the concept of trackability for dynamical games. We further develop an algorithm capable of dynamically tracking dynamical Nash equilibria and demonstrate its application in learning to cheat. Experimental results highlight the behavior of target-agents, pursuers, and adversaries within these dynamical adversarial scenarios. Our method offers a unified approach to navigating dynamic, adversarial environments, encompassing tasks such as evasion, capture, target assessment, and deception. These findings have broad practical implications, extending from board games like poker to complex domains involving autonomous agents. These networks are frequently exposed to various malicious attacks alongside unreliable communication channels, which can severely compromise service quality and user experience in critical applications like smart grids, smart healthcare, and autonomous driving. In response, numerous security mechanisms have been developed to address these threats. This survey comprehensively reviews state-of-the-art authentication and authorization mechanisms designed for IoT networks, detailing their core components, including protocols, methods, primitives, keys, security assumptions, attack models, threat models, and communication channel assumptions. It also provides a thematic analysis comparing these solutions across six dimensions: performance, functionality, usability, reliability, security, and availability. Ultimately, this survey offers valuable insights into the design and implementation of effective authentication and authorization systems for IoT networks. By examining existing solutions, identifying their limitations, and proposing potential improvements, we aim to guide future research in this field. These games are defined by a single bipartite distribution $p(a,b|x,y)$ with the constraint that it must be zero whenever at least one party receives a classical input from the other. We demonstrate that this class is not empty and identify a unique maximal element within it. This maximal game is characterized by a uniform distribution where the local winning probability is exactly zero. Furthermore, we establish that the CHSH game represents a special case of this classical asymmetric class. A direct consequence of our main theorem is that any distribution $p(x,y|a,b)$ that achieves the optimal value in a classical asymmetric nonlocal game necessarily reproduces the same optimal value in a standard symmetric nonlocal game. However, the converse does not hold. Finally, we investigate the relationship between these classical asymmetric games and fully classical simulations. We prove that any distribution achieving the optimal value in such a game can be effectively simulated by a classically conditioned distribution, $p'(a,b|c,x,y)$, which is deterministic ($p'(a,b|x,y) \in \{0,1\}$) and symmetric ($p'(a,b|x,y) = p'(b,a|y,x)$). The probability of a classical device succeeding in simulating an arbitrary distribution $p(x,y|a,b)$ is upper bounded by the best possible success rate achievable by such a conditionally symmetric distribution. Conversely, there exists an efficient procedure to construct a distribution that reaches this bound for any given $p(a,b|x,y)$. Consequently, the maximum nonlocal value of any classical asymmetric game corresponds to the minimum minimum error achievable by an asymmetric conditionally symmetric distribution. Furthermore, this maximum nonlocal value equals the maximum possible success probability for any classical distribution that can be simulated by a conditionally symmetric distribution. Collectively, these results indicate that classical asymmetric games serve as an ideal framework for investigating the boundaries of what can and cannot be simulated by conditionally symmetric distributions. Moreover, this class of games appears to be the most straightforward nonlocal distributions to extend into the quantum realm. Specifically, any quantum entanglement resource required to achieve the optimal quantum value in such a game can typically be established by introducing a single, trivial, classical, fully random, and completely decoupled variable into the nonlocal distribution. Therefore, these classical asymmetric games constitute the most fundamental nonlocal resources, making them ideal for examining the relationship between classical, quantum, and general nonlocal resources. This study concentrates on the electromagnetic response of quark-gluon plasma (QGP) within a magnetic field, analyzing electromagnetic radiation from this medium under various fluid expansion scenarios. We observe that the magnetic field significantly influences the emission of both charged and neutral particles, leading to the production of polarized photons and an enhanced rate of neutral radiation. These explicit expansion-dependent effects could potentially be utilized to assess the magnetic intensity of the colliding nuclei. Furthermore, we explicitly demonstrate that the polarization of photons generated in heavy-ion collisions is not isotropic in the laboratory frame; it is non-zero when the photon momentum forms an angle with the reaction plane. Our calculations indicate that the magnitude of this polarization is largest at intermediate transverse momenta. In conclusion, these results may provide additional methods for characterizing the QGP formed during collisions. Additionally, we note that our findings align with recent emissions computed by partonic kinetic theory in a magnetic field. However, a more precise comparison necessitates specific values for the magnetic field, which remain unavailable for current collider experiments. Such measurements could enable the estimation of the magnetic field within the QGP, offering insight into the initial state of the created fireball. Specifically, we established that the spectral function is directly proportional to the imaginary part of the in-medium photon self-energy. Employing this approximation, we derived an expression for the nuclear matter transport coefficient within the magnetic QGP. This paper introduces a novel, game-based methodology for training non-technical participants on the fundamentals of A/B testing. To establish the game's validity and reliability as a training tool, it was tested against traditional instruction methods. Our findings indicate that the proposed game significantly enhances participants' ability to answer knowledge-based questions compared to those receiving standard instructions. Furthermore, results demonstrate the game improves performance on practical tasks for non-technical users. These findings were derived from the largest study of its kind in the field, involving 756 participants. Additionally, by leveraging the 756 participants who received the game-based intervention, we developed robust generalizable models to predict performance, highlighting the game's utility for identifying user characteristics associated with better A/B testing competency. Finally, we discuss the study's contributions to the A/B testing field regarding the development of an effective, efficient, and scalable user training intervention. This research represents the first instance of applying a gaming approach to A/B testing training for non-technical individuals, while also being the largest such study conducted across the broader domain. The station integrates a two-mass mechanical system featuring both low-speed (2-pole) and high-speed (120-pole) generators. Low-speed turbines, powered by supersonic cross-flow nozzles, drive these generators to supply the DC generator with electricity. The nozzles are directly connected to the turbine shaft, which functions as a supersonic diffuser. Following compression and partial expansion within the nozzle blades, the nozzles are optimized to achieve the maximum possible shaft pressure ratio. The nozzles are arranged in 120 groups, each feeding a small 2-pole generator, with all generators linked in parallel to the high-speed generator, which supplies the total electrical load. The high-speed generator is connected to a magnetohydrodynamic pump driven by a 120-pole turbine, which is subsequently linked to a DC generator. The paper demonstrates that the DC generator achieves maximum power output when supplied by the nozzles under no-load nozzle conditions. Additionally, the high-speed generator is illustrated as supplying power to an emergency electrical network during nozzle no-load scenarios. This configuration represents a novel concept for a flexible, grid-independent microstation. The paper also examines the DC electrolysis process required to maximize hydrogen production. Furthermore, it is shown that this concept aligns with the second law of thermodynamics, thereby proving the configuration's feasibility. This study forms part of a broader initiative to address energy challenges, specifically exploring hydrogen production at the point of use.
