generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) approximation is essential for algorithms utilizing a local model to train deep neural networks. Current state-of-the-art approaches approximate the GGN's variance and skewness using outer products of gradients or Hessian-vector products, though these methods are computationally expensive and fail to scale effectively for networks containing convolutional layers. This paper introduces an alternative, data-dependent approximation of the GGN Hessian that leverages the sparse structure of the underlying computational graph to scale efficiently with respect to both the number of parameters ($p$) and the mini-batch size ($n$). Specifically, it targets an asymptotic complexity of $\mathcal{O}(np)$ by representing the GGN Grahm matrix through sums of rank-1 matrices, where the count of these rank-1 components depends on the dimension $p$ and batch size $n$ in a sparse manner. While construction costs are higher, they scale as $\mathcal{O}(n^2p^2/l)$ for a batch size $n$ and forward pass cost $l$. We demonstrate the utility of this methodology across various tasks, including linear regression, image classification, and semantic segmentation, where it serves as a practical metric for assessing model uncertainty. Our experimental findings indicate that, for specific applications, our approach yields more accurate estimates of statistical second-order descriptors compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. The associated software is available at github.com/loicfournier/ggn-rank1. We demonstrate that this phenomenon influences word representations, causing inanimate nouns of the same gender to cluster more closely together than those of different genders. Although "embedding debiasing" techniques prove ineffective at eliminating this bias, we show that carefully neutralizing gender signals within a word's context during training successfully removes it. Correcting this grammatical gender bias enhances the quality of resulting word embeddings in both monolingual and cross-lingual scenarios. We detail the most effective approach: employing multiple neutralizing filters alongside a standard projection filter within each word's context, trained in parallel. Crucially, this high-performing model remains simple, requiring only modifications to how words are represented within the network. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/joeymeyer/gender_bias. We further argue that previous research on gender bias in word embeddings may have inadvertently introduced this linguistic bias. While some prior works attempted to "gender neutralize" embeddings using various demographic terms, our findings indicate this strategy reinforces the bias. Instead, these studies would have achieved gender neutralization had they applied our method of neutralizing a specific signal within a well-defined context. This approach offers a straightforward alternative to previous complex and ineffective methods for removing various biases from word embeddings. Finally, we contend that our technique has broader applications for bias removal across NLP tasks. Although tasks often encode multiple, complex signals, addressing a single signal is a significant initial step toward creating fairer NLP systems. artificial intelligence has significantly advanced natural language processing. However, recent efforts have also introduced a previously unaddressed concern: adversarial attacks against deep neural networks used in text classification. Although these texts and methods remain robust in real-world scenarios, even minor perturbations can drastically decrease classifier accuracy. While this phenomenon is well-established in computer vision, text classification presents unique challenges due to its discrete nature. Perturbing individual words alters meaning, rendering it counterproductive, and generating entire sentences is computationally prohibitive. In contrast, altering just a few words is both effective and feasible. We present here a novel concept called "group perturbation," where multiple words are modified simultaneously to substantially reduce classifier accuracy. We detail a new attack strategy based on this principle and demonstrate, through experiments, that it surpasses state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. We validate the concept's success by achieving direction-level attacks, confirming that the technique works independently of both data and models. Furthermore, we evaluate the attack's practicality by measuring its scalability across various datasets and deep neural network architectures. Our findings indicate that group perturbation not only exceeds the performance of current state-of-the-art techniques but also proves more realistic, as it requires fewer words to be altered to cause misclassification. We release the group-perturbed SICK dataset to support future research in this domain. Although extensive research has addressed frequency dynamics, voltage behavior has often been overlooked. This study examines frequency and voltage stability in simple networks using linear stability analysis. We demonstrate both theoretically and through numerical simulations on both real and synthetic networks that voltage stability issues can emerge even when frequency issues do not, and vice versa. Specifically, network topology influences stability thresholds in both variables. Furthermore, in terms of topology, hubs facilitate earlier voltage stability issues, whereas increased conductance and decreased conductance variance promote earlier frequency problems. We examined these effects by altering various topological properties in variable networks. Finally, across all scenarios, voltage issues arise through a supercritical transcritical bifurcation, while frequency problems occur via a supercritical Hopf bifurcation. These findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of frequency and voltage dynamics, enabling more accurate modeling and analysis of power network stability. As a preliminary step, we conducted numerical simulations to evaluate how various topological features—such as conduction distribution, variance, variance of the degree variance, clustering, and assortativity—impact stability. These findings suggest that increasing conductance, particularly in well-connected networks, enhances overall system stability. This study provides a theoretical investigation of the electronic, topological, and superconducting characteristics of TMI structures built from two-dimensional Bi$_2$Se$_3$ sheets. Specifically, we examine twisted versions of the monolayer-stack trilayer (M215) and bilayer-stack bistrilayer (B230) models. While both M215 and B270 exhibit well-isolated surface bands near the Fermi level—enabling gate-tunable carrier densities and proximity-induced superconductivity—their twisted variants, M215-15° and B215-15°, display numerous in-plane bands. These horizontal bands facilitate gate-viable superconductivity via the proximity effect with a superconductor like Nb. Furthermore, these horizontal states are crucial for spin-orbit pairing, potentially driving unconventional superconductivity and topological phase transitions to new quantum-entangled phases in M215-15° and B215-15° twisted multilayers. Additionally, we explore further avenues for achieving novel quantum phenomena, such as quantum Hall effects and topologically nontrivial phases, in these twisted multilayer configurations. We also examine relevant structural, fabrication, and measurement challenges, concluding that the experimental realization of quantum phenomena in twisted multilayers of topological insulators is a viable and promising prospect. This work may facilitate the pursuit of new quantum phenomena, including quantum spin Hall effects and topological superconductivity, offering potential applications for topological superconducting qubits and Majorana zero modes. This research was conducted as an ex-post analysis. Although the proposal was submitted in the early stage of the moiré research field, the actual experimental and measurement efforts for materials like twisted TMI have yet to begin. The emerging research on quantum phenomena in twisted multilayers of topological insulators remains an exciting and promising area for future exploration. The branching fraction was determined to be ${\cal B}(\Sigma^+ \rightarrow p \mu^+ \mu^-) = (2.7 \pm 0.7 \pm 0.8) \times 10^{-10}$, where the first error is statistical and the second is systematic. This result aligns with the Standard Model prediction of $(2.5 \pm 3.2) \times 10^{-10}$. Additionally, the branching fraction for $\Sigma^+ \rightarrow p e^+ e^-$ was measured as $(1.9 \pm 1.0) b(\Lambda^0 : \Sigma^+)$, representing the initial observation of this decay. The ratio of $b(\Sigma^+ : \Lambda^0) / s(\Lambda^0 : \Sigma^+)$ was found to be $4.5 \pm 1.3$ (stat) $\pm 2.1$ (syst) $\pm 1.0$ (norm), consistent with Standard Model expectations. Furthermore, the ratio of $a(\Sigma^+ : \Lambda^0 : \Sigma^+)$ was constrained to $0.0 \pm 1.3$ (stat) $\pm 2.0$ (syst) $\pm 1.5$ (norm), also agreeing with Standard Model predictions. These findings support new tests of the Standard Model and provide data for studies of baryon mixing. The paper also includes a reevaluation of the $\Sigma^+ \rightarrow p e^+ e^-$ decay and an investigation into potential electromagnetic effects. This study investigates the influence of the magnetic field on plume characteristics within the plume collisionless reconnection regime, where the MHD approximation is invalid and the magnetic field is predominantly ideal. To achieve this, we conducted GEMRecon simulations to analyze two-plume collisions arising from magnetic reconnection between anti-parallel sheets. In this specific setup, the magnetic field in the inflow and outflow regions aligns with the inflow direction. Our findings indicate that the impact of the magnetic field on plume characteristics in this configuration is marginal. We also compared GEMRecon results with those from T3D simulations, observing that the two-plume collision signatures in GEMRecon simulations are less pronounced than in T3D simulations. This difference stems from the higher numerical viscosity in GEMRecon, which is insufficient to create a resistive layer. Consequently, these magnetic field effects should not hinder the detection of plume collisions as plasma instabilities in the plume collisionless reconnection regime. Finally, we concluded that using plume collisions to estimate the inflow reconnection rate is feasible for plume collisions occurring in the weakly collisional to collisionless reconnection regime. This conclusion holds because the magnetic field impact is significant when the inflow Alfvénic Mach number is low but diminishes to a negligible level as the inflow Alfvénic Mach number increases. Therefore, assessing the inflow Alfvénic Mach number is essential for reliably estimating the reconnection rate using the plume collision method. This research was conducted as part of the CME Multi-Wavelength Heliophysics (CMWH) initiative, which aims to enhance our understanding of solar eruptions by integrating data from various spacecraft and ground-based observatories. Specifically, this work represents the contribution of the Solar Orbiter mission within the CMWH framework. The research was carried out using GEMRecon simulations. GEMRecon is a three-dimensional, ideal MHD particle-in-cell code developed by the Group for Electromagnetic Theory for Space Research at the University of Central Florida. It employs a Lagrangian grid framework featuring adaptive mesh refinement capabilities. The code employs a second-order Godunov method for the hydrodynamic component and utilizes an HLL-based Riemann solver for the MHD component. For more details, visit the GEMRecon website. This includes not only the bending of light rays but also the finite width of atmospheric gradients, resulting in images of refracted objects becoming both displaced and blurred. This paper presents preliminary findings from ground-based imaging experiments using two cameras with hardware differences to measure quantities related to blurring and shift. These metrics will be utilized to formulate and validate a Gaussian model describing the relationship between the atmospheric point-spread function (PSAD) and ultimately, the atmospheric dispersion function (ADF). While numerous existing ADF parametrizations exist for spectroscopic applications, this work focuses on developing a Gaussian-based parametrization of the PSAD to quickly generate representative models. This approach is particularly advantageous for systems employing a camera array. The primary objective is to characterize best-fit parametrizations for each camera in a array to determine local ADFs, thereby enabling the derotation of spectra. Future efforts will compare various ADF models to identify the optimal choice, accounting for computational costs versus characterization accuracy. Additionally, this method can be adapted for tomographic observations of fast-evolving phenomena, such as supernovae. Tomography aims to reduce blurred images to 2D slices, reconstructing 3D structures from projections. Specifically, this approach could facilitate the tomographic observation of supernovae around the time of maximum brightness. In such scenarios, a large number of cameras would be employed to characterize local ADFs, analogous to how CT scanners utilize a array of detectors. Characterizing these ADFs is crucial for accurately reconstructing projections. Ultimately, a array-based method for representing local ADFs will be developed to support tomographic supernova observations. Specifically, we define a continuous abelian group as an abelian group equipped with a topology where every non-trivial element possesses a non-trivial continuous character; this topic is covered in Section 2. In Section 3, we introduce the category of topological abelian groups and the category of pure abelian groups (those with flat quotient by torsion), demonstrating that the map from free topological abelian groups to abelian groups factors through a duality functor from the former category to the latter. We prove that this functor establishes an equivalence between the category of locally compact abelian groups and abelian groups, thereby providing a proof of the Pontryagin duality theorem. Finally, in Section 4, we examine extensions of this result, including the cases of locally linear topological spaces and topological modules over topological rings. All arguments rely exclusively on basic set theory and elementary algebraic and topological properties of abelian groups, avoiding advanced tools such as Stone spaces or model theory. We believe this proof is more direct and simpler than those found in existing literature. Our goal is to demonstrate that Pontryagin duality can be proven using elementary methods and to offer a didactically oriented proof suitable for a broad audience. We aim for this approach to be more accessible than proofs relying on Stone–Čech compactification or Stone spaces, which are typically reserved for advanced treatments of topological groups. We trust that our elementary approach will be at least as effective as those found in textbooks. Our objective is to present a proof suitable for students with a background in abstract algebra, perhaps supplemented by a minimal introduction to topology. Network (WPCN), where a multi-antenna power beacon (PB) transmits a dedicated energy signal to a wireless device, which subsequently communicates with a destination using the harvested energy. In this framework, the PB emits energy signals only when the destination lacks transmit power, while simultaneously receiving data from the user. We formulate an optimization problem aimed at maximizing the system's long-term throughput, subject to constraints on transmit power, energy causality, interference limits, and communication quality of service (QoS). For scenarios where the PB possesses channel state information (CSI) regarding the user-destination link, we develop an efficient Lagrange dual decomposition-based solution. Conversely, in cases where such information is unavailable at the PB, we address the challenge of unknown parameters through adaptive learning. In this context, we propose a data-driven approach that employs adaptive learning to estimate hidden variables and apply the dual decomposition-based optimization. Simulation results validate that the proposed methods achieve significant performance improvements, with the data-driven technique delivering a 10.5% extra throughput gain compared to traditional designs when PB channel information is unavailable. Furthermore, we demonstrate the computational efficiency of the learning-based algorithm by analyzing its training time and execution time. Finally, we evaluate the throughput performance in the presence of estimation errors, confirming the robustness of the proposed learning-based methodology. These findings highlight the substantial benefits of integrating learning techniques with intelligent IRS-assisted WPCNs, particularly under conditions of imperfect channel information. This work offers a solid foundation for future research in learning-enabled intelligent wireless systems. Keywords: Learning-enabled intelligent wireless systems, Wireless powered communication network (WPCN), Internet of Reconfigurable Reflective Surface (IRS), Beamforming optimization. within a unified $A_4$ flavor-symmetry framework. In this model, the dark matter candidate emerges from the dark sector and mirrors the structure of leptonic mixing parameters in the visible sector. The scale of dark matter production is closely tied to the mass of the right-handed neutrino, which simultaneously dictates the magnitude of leptogenesis. We provide detailed predictions for dark matter abundance, leptogenesis, and direct detection scattering off nuclei. Our findings indicate that viable dark matter halos with masses exceeding those of the top quark lead to suppressed leptogenesis, thereby constraining the scale of heavy right-handed neutrinos. Conversely, for dark matter masses comparable to or lighter than the tera-electron volt range, substantial leptogenesis becomes feasible, particularly when the dark matter mass hovers near $1\,\textrm{TeV}$. These results offer a promising pathway to establish a robust link between the origins of dark matter and leptogenesis. Additionally, our model offers accurate predictions for the leading-order scattering cross section with nuclei, aligning well with recent experimental data from XENON1T and LVD. Furthermore, we demonstrate a natural correlation between the fermionic dark matter annihilation cross section and its thermal relic density, resulting in values consistent with WMAP and Planck observations. Finally, our framework successfully reproduces the leptogenesis requirement $m_{N_1} \gtrsim 10^{9}\,\textrm{GeV}$, thereby elucidating the connection between real-time baryon asymmetry and heavy right-handed neutrino masses. This work suggests an alternative explanation for the suppression of CP asymmetry in neutrino oscillations, distinct from resonant leptogenesis. We anticipate that these outcomes serve as a valuable foundation for interpreting upcoming dark matter detection signals and neutrino experiments. We also express gratitude to L. J. This study investigates the higher-spin generalization of the bootstrap approach for $\mathcal{N} = 4$ SUSY Toda theory, demonstrating that the three-point function is defined by dimensional analysis and central charges. Consequently, the bootstrap approach establishes a direct link between higher-spin correlators and stress tensor correlators. Furthermore, we examine a specific limit corresponding to an $\mathcal{N} = 1$ field theory reduction, where the resulting correlators are interpreted within $\mathcal{N} = 1$ SUSY Yang-Mills supermultiplets. Finally, we implement the bootstrap method for the superconformal generalization of the $\mathcal{N} = 1$ SUSY Yang-Mills multiplet in four-dimensional Euclidean space. In this context, the three-point functions are determined either by dimensional analysis or by reducing from a four-dimensional $\mathcal{N} = 4$ SUSY vector multiplet. Networks (GANs) for creating realistic images, GANs frequently fail to converge steadily. We contend that this instability stems from training on high-dimensional image data, which obscures crucial low-dimensional information regarding image semantics. Consequently, we propose that stabilizing GAN training is achievable by projecting both real and generated images into low-dimensional manifolds to determine whether they belong to a specific data category. Within this framework, GANs serve as a tool to learn the mappings between these real and generated manifolds. Representing the GAN as a three-way game between the manifold mappings and two manifold discriminators, we develop a comprehensive training framework that includes complete theoretical proofs and experimental results validating our hypotheses. This approach not only yields semantically meaningful low-dimensional representations but also produces images of higher quality than those from traditional GANs. Our complete open-source code is available for reference and use. To our knowledge, this presents a novel and unified methodology for estimating image data through manifold mappings. Empirically, our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods. We anticipate that this research will offer new perspectives for future investigations into GANs and image generation. These algebras are shown to be isomorphic to a specific type of continuous function algebra. Specifically, for the unit disk, the algebra of such operators with continuous symbols is isomorphic to the Dixmier algebra of $n$-variable continuous functions on a compact space $K$ vanishing at infinity. The space $K$ is defined as the inverse image of a point under a continuous map from the $n$-torus to a $d$-torus, where $n-d$ equals the topological complexity of an $n$-dimensional disk with boundary glued to itself. For the unit circle, the algebra of these operators is isomorphic to a commutative $C^*$-algebra of continuous functions on the $n$-torus.

The paper addresses two primary questions: first, it derives a formula for the dimension of this commutative $C^*$-algebra; second, it calculates the algebraic dimension of the algebra of $n$-variable Toeplitz operators with continuous symbols acting on $L^2$ over an $n$-circle, providing explicit basis elements and a description of all elements. These findings significantly advance the understanding of non-self-adjoint operator algebras. Additionally, the study determines the algebra of multipliers for the algebra of bounded Toeplitz operators on the space of analytic functions in the disk and provides a description of their Jordan content. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the dimension and algebraic dimension of the algebra of $n$-variable Toeplitz operators are equal and correspond to the topological complexity of an $n$-disk, a value computed via a recursive formula established in the paper. All methodologies employed rely heavily on algebraic topology and homotopy theory to resolve key problems within operator theory. Additionally, it is proven that every ideal in the algebra of $n$-variable Toeplitz operators is a principal ideal generated by a single projection operator. Finally, the work clarifies which Toeplitz operators are weakly compact and identifies a specific subclass of symbols for which the corresponding Toeplitz operators remain compact. Additionally, it is established that the algebra of these Toeplitz operators contains no non-trivial ideal with a trivial commutant. This hyper-energetic plasma cannot originate from the star alone; we demonstrate that it results from shocks generated by cloud material deflected off stellar winds or from X-ray-induced photoevaporation of cloud surface clouds. To identify the physical mechanism responsible for producing this high-temperature plasma, we employ hydrodynamical simulations that model X-ray beam heating of a plane parallel to S1's cloud surface. These mechanisms can yield a spectrum with a high-energy tail reaching temperatures above $100$ keV, provided that approximately $10^{19}$ erg of energy is deposited over a period of $10^6$ years. We argue that invoking coronal loops or collisions with comet-like objects are unnecessary to explain the observed extreme X100 component. Furthermore, we highlight that within the broader context of star formation, these shocks and the CO molecules absorbing the X-rays are integral outcomes of the process. Finally, the implications of this mechanism for the Rho Ophiuchi cloud and its planetary systems, along with the broader astrobiological significance, will be explored. While numerous models exist for this purpose, selecting the most appropriate one remains a challenging task, particularly when dealing with diverse datasets. Although recent research has attempted to address this, many existing solutions rely on ad-hoc procedures or are restricted to specific data types. This study investigates whether an automated and customizable method can universally identify the forecasting model best suited for a given time series. We address this by adapting a well-known machine learning framework to directly estimate a model's performance on unseen test data. Subsequently, we outline a comprehensive procedure to extend this framework for selecting both the forecasting model and its hyperparameters. Employing a recently introduced unified supermodel for time series forecasting, we demonstrate how a specific algorithm can automatically select hyperparameters across various datasets. Furthermore, a specialized procedure tailored for a specific data type can recommend a more suitable model. Our results indicate that a unified approach can effectively identify high-performing models across a broad range of datasets, while reconfiguring existing frameworks can adapt this method for specific data types. Finally, an extension of a recent procedure for selecting neural network architectures for CNN-RNN models has been developed based on experimental evaluations. This type of extension offers a universal solution for problems where ad-hoc methods currently dominate. These findings underscore the necessity of creating automated selection procedures to complement the ongoing development of new, state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, the proposed method serves as a template for adapting existing approaches to utilize a wider variety of models. Millions and Powerball draw more participants, thereby raising the chance of multiple winners sharing the pot. Consequently, as the probability of collisions—where two or more buyers hold identical winning tickets—rises, the expected value (EV) of a lottery ticket declines. This study introduces an analytical framework to calculate the EV of a single ticket and the likelihood of a collision for various ticket counts within a specific draw, accounting for the "hot spot" effect. This effect occurs when the lottery operator intentionally loads the drum with multiple copies of a ticket, an occasional strategy employed to facilitate the sale of several tickets simultaneously. Our method is exact and relies solely on knowing the number of distinct tickets, a figure typically disclosed by operators. By leveraging this data, we derive lower and upper bounds that remain tight when the number of available tickets significantly exceeds the number of players. Furthermore, our approach remains accurate even when the probability of a ticket being selected is not uniform. Applying our formulas reveals that for typical participant and ticket volumes, the relative error of previously used approximations (which ignore collisions) can reach up to 20 percent. We introduce a simple approximation formula for EV and collision probability that matches ordinal accuracy in terms of ticket types and cardinal accuracy regarding the EV; it is ordinal and cardinal accurate regarding collisions and is at most 2 percent off the true EV when the ticket pool is substantially larger than the number of available types. Finally, we examine how ignoring "hot spots" influences these metrics and suggest methods to quantify the associated errors. Keywords: Expected value, collisions, Ramsey theory, Poincaré principle. The analysis is conducted within a simplified cubic crystal structure possessing at least a diamond lattice, which facilitates the problem's three-dimensional nature by utilizing only a single acoustic phonon branch. Our findings reveal that the forward-going angular momentum-transferring interaction yields the most significant temperature-dependent corrections to the superconducting gap and critical temperature, particularly at low temperatures where the gap is minimal. These forward-going interactions are prevalent in both isotropic and anisotropic superconducting states. Furthermore, at any specified temperature, the maximum temperature-dependent reduction in the superconducting order parameter occurs precisely at the momentum where the phonon-mediated effective electron-electron interaction is weakest. In the isotropic case, this minimum effectiveness corresponds to a scattering angle of 90 degrees. Conversely, for $p$-wave states, the forward-going angular momentum-transferring interaction serves as the baseline effect, resulting in an increase in the superconducting order parameter as temperature rises. This low-value gap exists at the momentum where the phonon-mediated effect is strongest. Finally, the conclusions regarding the nature of these electron-acoustic-phonon coupling mechanisms are demonstrated to hold true for all single acoustic phonon branches in a diamond lattice and remain applicable to all three-dimensional superconducting systems. Consequently, these results present potentially testable predictions for specific materials. Ultimately, these findings may aid in elucidating various phenomena associated with non-phononic superconductivity, such as the anomalous temperature-dependent behavior observed in cuprate high-$T_c$ materials. It operates under the premise that data are unstructured, meaning specific locations are not inherently meaningful; for instance, in image data, the distance between adjacent pixels is conceptually minimal. To align with this assumption, the algorithm models data as a collection of local neighborhoods and captures local structures by analyzing the statistical independence of joint distributions between paired points. However, because data are assumed to be local in nature, long-range or global dependencies between distant points are underrepresented. Since the relevance of data often extends beyond local scopes, we propose capturing global structures by leveraging long-term correlations between pairs of points. This study introduces iTSNE (informer-based t-SNE), which integrates the informer architecture to extract global correlations and substantially boosts embedding performance. Specifically, by integrating the informer's additional paths into t-SNE's affinity matrix, we generate affinity matrices enriched with both local and global correlations. Consequently, the resulting embedding better reflects global correlations, thereby enhancing performance. We evaluated this approach on three real-world datasets, demonstrating that the informer+TSNE framework significantly surpasses baseline methods. Additionally, we conducted image reconstruction from the generated embeddings, confirming that the informer+TSNE framework effectively captures long-range correlations and yields substantial improvements over baseline approaches. Our goal is to build a comprehensive model that characterizes how work stress connects to an employee's multi-dimensional health profile. This characterization enables the identification of employee segments that exhibit similar stress-health relationships, offering insights useful for designing tailored wellness programs. We evaluated several models using both simulated and real-world datasets, with the real data collected from a sample of 344 remote employees via an online survey. Our results demonstrate that these characterization and segmentation models can significantly enhance our understanding of the complex, non-linear link between work stress and the diverse range of physical, cognitive, and emotional health issues employees face. Ultimately, this improved understanding can support the creation of personalized wellness initiatives for remote workers. The analysis focused on the midrapidity region ($|y|<0.8$) within midcentral Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV, covering centralities from 10% to 70%. The study selected events with transverse momentum $0.15 < p_{\rm T} < 2.5$ GeV/$c$ and identified $D$ mesons via their decay products $D^0\to K^-\pi^+$ and $D^+\to K^- \pi^+ \pi^+$, while vector mesons were analyzed through $K^*$ ($\to K^{\pi} \pi$), $\rho$ ($\to \pi \pi$), and $\phi$ ($\to s$) decay channels. The results indicate that the $v_2$ of light hadrons (pions and kaons) is well-described by energy-dependent transport coefficients ($\eta/s$) in a hydrodynamic model. Conversely, the $v_2$ of vector mesons suggests an increased $\eta/s$ above 0.1 GeV/$c$, with those having $p_{\rm T}>1$ GeV/c exhibiting elastic scattering properties. Finally, the $v_2$ of $D$ mesons is also examined to explore potential deviations from the leading particle scenario. This study represents the first elliptic flow analysis of mesons across different spin categories in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV. (7 pages, 5 figures)

The extensive implementation of Big Data and the proliferation of online transactions have left extensive process traces in corporate environments, enabling the automatic extraction of these traces from various process logs. Although numerous algorithms and tools exist for estimating Process Mining Processes (PMPro) from such logs, reverse-engineering PMPro from physical artifacts remains challenging and is frequently necessary when digital trace extraction is impractical. This paper introduces a method to extract process traces from PDF files and applies it to a large-scale dataset of 147,575 invoices from a bank. We subsequently compare two machine learning techniques applied to this data to reverse-engineer PMPro. The results demonstrate that utilizing PDFs for PMPro estimation yields encouraging outcomes, suggesting potential future applications.

This paper demonstrates two key findings: first, the maximum value of $\lambda$ for which a probability measure exists is determined by the spectral radius of the kernel function on the domain $[0,\lambda^{1/d}]$. Second, a Monte Carlo algorithm can efficiently generate samples from this measure when the density is analytic on $\mathbb{C}^n$. These findings are validated through numerical experiments. Notably, this approach facilitates a new Monte Carlo method for evaluating the density of states in frustrated systems, using an example of an analytic Strauss process on the torus to illustrate this application. The analysis relies on the Chebyshev radius of the Strauss kernel, for which we provide both theoretical upper bounds and a numerical upper bound within a finite-dimensional approximation. Leveraging these results, we prove sample-complexity bounds for specific Strauss processes. One such process involves interacting spins on a torus with a kernel derived from the Fourier transform of a Bessel function; this model can represent analytically integrable systems, such as one-dimensional spin systems or non-interacting quantum many-body systems. Consequently, our findings yield exact Monte Carlo sampling and a rapidly converging estimate of the density of states for these systems in the thermodynamic limit. This capability is achieved by effectively bounding the number of samples required to achieve a target accuracy. Additionally, our techniques enable a Monte Carlo computation of the sign problem, with potential ramifications for Monte Carlo simulations of fermionic gases. Finally, we identify a specific class of Strauss processes for which sampling is efficient in any dimension. These processes possess a kernel that is a "separable function of separable variables," a property that encompasses well-known examples like the Ising model and a simplified quantum non-interacting model. We also demonstrate that these Strauss processes can be extended to define Strauss-type measures on manifolds. This extension enables general Monte Carlo sampling on manifolds like spheres and ensures a finite convergence rate for sampling in thermodynamic limits on manifolds where the kernel is a positive-definite function. While pressure sensors offer a potential solution by enabling precise measurement of soil interaction forces, their practical implementation has thus far been limited. In this study, we introduce PSOT (Point-Spring Orthogonal Torsion Spring Tool), a novel mechanism designed to integrate external pressure data into closed-loop locomotion control systems. PSOT features a toroidal pressure interface that compresses against the ground under the influence of gravity, allowing for the direct measurement of contact pressure at every point. Simulations utilizing both soft (compressed soil) and hard ground representations were conducted to evaluate its performance. Furthermore, a physical simulation incorporating PSOT's pressure interface proved effective for designing a running control strategy suitable for complex, uneven soft soil terrains. These findings suggest that PSOT serves as a viable framework for high-performance locomotion on soft soils. This report offers a comprehensive overview of key areas within quantum machine learning by demonstrating various quantum learning algorithms that surpass classical ones under specific conditions. By synthesizing these examples into broader principles, we derive general theorems that illustrate potential quantum speedups for diverse learning tasks. Subsequently, experimental evidence supports these theoretical findings, confirming practical quantum advantages in machine learning. Finally, possessing a robust understanding of these experimental limitations establishes a crucial foundation for developing more robust future quantum machine learning algorithms. In this manner, we demonstrate that quantum machine learning is a viable application area capable of achieving immediate quantum supremacy. Furthermore, a detailed examination of accompanying experiments highlights the specific resources required for these immediate wins, aiding in the assessment of potential bottlenecks inherent to current quantum learning algorithms. Leveraging this insight, we propose strategies to mitigate these limitations through hybrid approaches combining classical and quantum machine learning. This proposal represents a novel perspective on quantum machine learning that has been previously unexplored. Through theoretical results, experimental validation, and methodological suggestions, we provide a complete framework for understanding contemporary quantum machine learning. Collectively, our findings illustrate that quantum machine learning holds the potential to deliver quantum advantages that are both accessible and practical. Consequently, we conclude that quantum machine learning constitutes a vital component of the broader quest for quantum supremacy. Our preprint reports 296 citations across 141 countries, establishing it as one of the most widely read theoretical papers in quantum science (https://inspirehep.net/spi/1988473). The following review aims to consolidate these efforts, synthesizing theoretical insights with experimental realities to present a holistic view of the field. fragile structures formed from sparse particle aggregates, are widely utilized in food, pharmaceutical, biomedical, and numerous industrial sectors. This study examines the viscoelastic and rheological characteristics of two such gels: one comprising "sticky" particles and the other "non-sticky" particles that undergo weak attractive crystalline phase separation. Our findings reveal a striking reorientation in both gels when a constant stress is applied: the storage modulus ($G'$) initially declines before ultimately rising. In the case of the "sticky" particle gel, this behavior stems from the rapid breakup of large aggregates into smaller, more flexible ones due to shear, followed by thermal ripening that causes the average particle size to increase. Conversely, in the phase separation gel of "non-sticky" particles, shear retardation accelerates the separation dynamics, causing small particles to settle at the bottom and large particles to accumulate at the top, thereby increasing the volume fraction of the attractive phase and enhancing rigidity. These processes are investigated using a combination of numerical simulations and theoretical modeling. We present a unified framework that accounts for shear-induced particle sedimentation, aggregation, and gel growth in systems exhibiting attractive colloidal phase separation. By explaining how pre-gel separation dynamics critically influence the macroscopic rheological properties, this work offers conceptual insights applicable to various both natural and engineered colloidal materials. Furthermore, it establishes a pathway for the independent control of a gel's mechanical and optical attributes, which could significantly advance material design. Finally, we outline future research directions aimed at creating gels with non-trivial microstructures that display both spatially varying mechanical properties and color variations. This approach holds the potential to generate self-assembling, shadow-casting smart materials with applications in sensing and imaging. We anticipate that these concepts will inspire novel research at the intersection of colloidal science, materials science, and soft photonics. We conclude by expressing hope that this will serve as a catalyst for new discoveries. Specifically, we establish the validity of the conjecture for $2^m$, noting that the number of required verifications grows proportionally to $m$. Our focus is on designing strategies that achieve a positive probability of satisfying Hall's condition within a specific timeframe, even when an adversary controls a subset of agents and deliberately creates redundant connections to obscure true agent locations. This presents a significant challenge for verification, particularly given a large network where identifying all neighbors is impractical. Specifically, we examine scenarios where agents possess only local visibility and the adversary is aware of the total count of distinct neighbors. We propose a strategy featuring a corresponding "stop-the-bleeding" verification method capable of rapidly detecting violations of Hall's condition. Our primary finding is that verifying the absence of violations in local networks is fundamentally harder than verifying their occurrence. However, we demonstrate that for structured networks featuring a core of highly connected agents, the probability of violation detection can be significantly enhanced. These conclusions are drawn from extensions of a probabilistic model originally developed to match unmanned aerial vehicles with targets. By establishing upper and lower bounds on the time required to detect violations, we reveal substantial disparities in both fundamental and local detectability. Fundamentally, the difficulty arises because the optimal adversary strategy involves forcing a subset of agents to have fewer than $s$ distinct neighbors for some $s$. Locally, however, the challenge shifts to an adversary that randomly removes edges, making violations harder to detect and resulting in weaker bounds. These findings suggest that networks with dense cores are more suitable for matching agents to targets. Furthermore, this research holds potential application for chemical agents needing to verify that every subset possesses a distinct neighbor to effectively disperse a chemical signature across a region. This capability is crucial for verification as a prerequisite for using dense cores to eliminate ambiguity. To achieve this, agents must first match with local targets to ensure a positive probability of satisfying Hall's condition. Additionally, this methodology supports the development of efficient algorithms for unmanned aerial vehicle target tracking. The difficulty in detecting violations is particularly notable for sparsely connected agents. This systematic failure suggests that requiring the model to explicitly attend to specific linguistic features could mitigate the issue. Consequently, we introduce a straightforward yet impactful framework called Position Encoded Attention (PEA). This framework integrates positional encodings directly into the self-attention mechanisms of the standard encoder-decoder architecture. PEA yields consistent performance improvements, establishing a new state-of-the-art for English-to-German NMT using subword bytepair encoding within an attention-based Transformer model. Consequently, these findings demonstrate practical applications for both fact enhancement and functional constraint enforcement within transformer-based NMT systems. Both our preliminary analysis and the encoded data are publicly accessible to facilitate additional investigation into emergent biases within transformer-based NMT systems. Our modifications achieve a new SOTA for English-to-German NMT using subword BPE within a transformer attention mechanism. By directly reducing these specific factual errors, Position Encoded Attention (PEA) integrates positional encodings into positions within self-attention mechanisms. Positional encodings encode relative or sequential information within a sequence. By embedding this information into the attention mechanism, the model gains explicit knowledge regarding positional data within both the encoder and decoder sequences. This approach offers a straightforward method to enhance performance while eliminating the need for emergent attention heads or complex architectural overhauls.

Question-Answer Pairs (QAPs) serve as a prevalent method for evaluating the quality of WOLs by linking semantic elements to natural language descriptions. Beyond facilitating human quality assessment, these analysis results serve as valuable inputs for further automated quality enhancement. Additionally, we have made the generated QAPs publicly accessible to support research and development.

In contrast, this study demonstrates through direct numerical simulations of an isotropically forced, rotating, inviscid two-dimensional flow that the flow naturally develops coherent structures rotating at vastly different rates across a range of scales. These scales are determined by the flow's initial turbulence. The coherent motions exhibit inverse energy cascades and geostrophic balances, driven by rotation at every scale. This research represents the first investigation into self-organized scale generation in a rotating two-dimensional fluid. The identified mechanism is fundamental to various geophysical and astrophysical phenomena governed by large-scale coherent structures, such as the Earth's deep oceans, core, and envelope. Additionally, the mechanism described in this study is distinct from the anti-diffusive scale generation observed in two-dimensional MHD, despite both phenomena occurring in different models featuring large-scale coherent structures and inverse scale evolution. The model employed here may facilitate the construction of sub-cospectral reduced-order models. By leveraging the scale invariance of the identified mechanism, these models can be enhanced by including geostrophic modes and resolution-independent subgrid-scale models. This approach could significantly improve the accuracy of forecasting and control strategies for geophysical and astrophysical turbulent flows. Specifically, we examine the impact of spin spin-polarization (SSP)—a technique previously demonstrated to yield superior accuracy in strongly correlated systems compared to Coulomb correlation—within a spin unrestricted framework for the simple cubic Strontium Vanadium Oxide. Starting with a spin-polarized configuration at one vanadium atom's site within a unit cell, SSP propagates spin polarizations across the lattice while employing a Hartree-Fock (HF) one-electron mean field. Our results indicate that this HF-SSP approach generates a spin ordered state with alternating up and down columns of Vanadium atoms, corresponding to an antiferromagnetic (AFM) structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SSP profoundly influences the effective one-electron Hamiltonian, revealing that spin self-interaction errors significantly compromise Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) calculations even under collinear spin assumptions. These insights motivate the use of SSP-correction methods, such as HF-SSP, to mitigate DFT's spin self-interaction errors and attain a closer approximation to exact DFT outcomes. Finally, we show that applying HF-SSP in conjunction with VMC successfully overcomes these challenges, producing results approximately 0.4 eV more precise than those obtained from standard DFT. Additionally, we observe that the HF-SSP method profoundly alters the band structure of Sr$_2$VO$_3$, transforming it from a metallic state predicted by DFT into a magnetic insulator characterized by a 1.2 eV gap. All computational procedures were executed using the OpenMX software suite. These findings contribute to the growing recognition of HF-SSP as a significant advancement in achieving high-precision calculations involving Coulomb correlated systems. We anticipate that HF-SSP will stimulate further research aimed at fully leveraging its potential for highly accurate electronic structure computations. This study presents an analysis examining the gullibility of gPT-3 towards such content. By analyzing these variations, we evaluated how lattice cut-offs modify finite-temperature phase transitions, transition orders, and the emergence of decoupling in the heavy coupling regime. Our findings reveal that the $Z_1$ component of the decoupling subgroup governs the first-order transition and correctly predicts the transition's transition-point temperature, $T_c\approx200$ MeB, even near the lower lattice cut-off of $k_{max}\approx0.5$ GeV. Furthermore, the results indicate that the $Z_1$-invariant subgroup dominates the phase transition, leading to a transition that is neither fully first- nor zero-order but lies between the two. Additionally, we demonstrate that the critical temperature remains independent of the lattice time extent $N_t$. Finally, based on these outcomes, we discuss the implications for QCD's low-temperature phase. u$-model is introduced as a substitute for the complex Boltzmann collision operator. Adhering to the relaxation-time approximation, this model defines a collision frequency $
u$ as any positive, Mach number-dependent function. This framework circumvents the limitations of the BGK model, as the constant collision frequency in the $
u$-model does not rely on the specific molecular interaction potential. By utilizing the Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (BGK) model as a foundation, the study also develops an $\omega$-model, where $\omega$ represents a constant collision frequency. These kinetic models are solved using Lattice Boltzmann methods on a single-relaxation-time lattice to obtain local macroscopic variables. The resulting schemes exhibit superlinear stability under appropriate boundary conditions and can incorporate various body forces by adding corresponding terms to the discrete Boltzmann equation. This work further demonstrates the application of both the $
u$-model and the $\omega$-model to calculate macroscopic properties in rarefied gas dynamics, specifically examining slip flow, thermal creep, and Poiseuille flow within a channel under rarefied conditions. Results are compared against Boltzmann solution data, the BGK model, direct simulation Monte Carlo results, experimental data, and previous theoretical findings. Ultimately, the $
u$-model and $\omega$-model demonstrate greater accuracy, broader applicability, and higher efficiency than the BGK model. Furthermore, this approach paves the way for dynamic kinetic modeling using the $

This paper introduces an exact inference algorithm for open-domain semantic parsing. The stability of this novel structure was confirmed through first-principles calculations. While Gd$_5$Ge$_4$ is metallic at room temperature, its susceptibility decreases across the Curie temperature, consistent with itinerant magnetism. The transition is governed by the collapse of electron holes near the Fermi level in the conduction band, specifically near the ${\rm K}$ point, which exhibit high density of states. At low temperatures, the susceptibility is dominated by dipole-dipole interactions between Gd moments, resulting in a -0.6 emu/K$^2$ temperature dependence and a broad maximum in ac susceptibility, characteristics typical of metallic ferromagnets. The orbital-decomposed total magnetic susceptibility, incorporating both dipole-dipole interaction and orbital quenching effects, aligns well with experimental uncertainties, confirming that the Gd $2p$ orbital contributes significantly to the temperature dependence. Furthermore, the Landau free energy analysis indicates robust ferromagnetic order due to high Landau coefficients and a substantial energy barrier for phase transitions. Finally, the molecular field theory predicts a transition temperature of 125 K, which closely matches the experimental value of 118 K, while molecular dynamics simulations yield a finding of 120 K, indicating good overall agreement. Ultimately, Gd$_5$Ge$_4$ represents a promising candidate for studying the magnetic properties of metallic ferromagnets. This paper clarifies the relationship between these special functions and the discrete parameter-deformed Heun equation (DPE), demonstrating that both entities can be derived from a single inhomogeneous Differential-Difference equation. This unified differential-difference equation features a set of discrete parameters that correspond to both the distinct sets of discrete parameters inherent to the DCHE and the DPE. Specifically, the deformed parameter sets for the DCHE and DPE can be viewed as strictly chiral subsets within this unified framework. Consequently, singular and irregular singular points emerge within a discrete plane defined by these chiral discrete parameters. The specific functions and standard Heun equation are recovered when the discrete parameters are set to zero. Furthermore, this perspective offers a novel interpretation of the convergence domains for the special functions. Additionally, it is shown that for particular choices of the discrete parameters, the DCHE and DPE can be transformed into ordinary differential equations, thereby generating special functions and polynomial sequences, respectively. Finally, a specific instance of discrete parameter-deformed Heun equations, the Meixner-Papkov equation, is explored in connection with discrete orthogonal polynomials. This connection provides an alternative derivation and a new source of special functions for discrete orthogonal polynomials, while also offering a fresh interpretation of their associated parameters. Additionally, it is observed that under a specific choice of discrete parameters, a single equation can assume the forms of both the DCHE and DPE simultaneously, resulting in a family of semi-deformed Heun equations and their associated special functions. The proposed controller is distributed in two key aspects: (i) each agent independently designs an observer to approximate the plant's output map, and (ii) the control inputs are generated in a distributed manner through the arithmetic geometric mean algorithm applied to the estimated maps. A critical advantage is that the communication topology required for the agents to reach consensus is significantly simpler than that needed when agents possess full plant access. This simplicity stems from the fact that each agent only needs to estimate its local parameter rather than the global one, and the topology for agreeing on the average of these local parameters. Consequently, the method is effective for embedded control systems where communicating full plant data is impractical, instead relying on agents to estimate and utilize local parameters. Finally, this approach is also applicable to identifying parameters of interconnected dynamical systems using persistent excitation input data. Although significant progress has been made in various subfields, such as social influence diffusion, a comprehensive review of a real-world system's complete lifecycle—from concept generation and implementation to long-term behavioral analysis—remains a paramount goal. Concept generation involves selecting appropriate data sources and representation methods to build a network that accurately reflects the real-world system. However, many existing network systems suffer from issues like sparse or incomplete data, leading to networks that fail to capture the true system dynamics. To address this, we propose Graph-Switched Autoencoders (GSA), a method designed for topological inference that analyzes networks as a collection of constituent graphs rather than a single static representation. Specifically, GSA enables the disentanglement of noise and signal within observed networks and facilitates the inference of latent, dynamic topological connections. We demonstrate that GSA surpasses established state-of-the-art topological inference techniques by introducing a novel application: a topological insight-driven model of COVID-19 spread. This case study reveals that incorporating both social and transportation networks provides more accurate explanations for COVID-19 spread compared to using either network in isolation. Furthermore, we outline key directions for future research in this data-centric area. As graph neural networks continue to dominate topological inference, understanding methodological choices regarding data aggregation and representation is crucial for researchers working with real-world data. In this regard, GSA offers a unified, rigorous, and interpretable framework for inferring both the existence and structure of networks. We anticipate that this work will provide valuable inspiration for both application-oriented and methodological advancements in the field of graph neural networks. eco-evolutionary biology) focuses on the mutual influence between ecological processes and the variation, selection, and inheritance of heritable traits within populations. This interdisciplinary area encompasses various sub-disciplines, such as adaptive dynamics, evolutionary game theory, and evolutionarily significant traits, which collectively explore different facets of these interactions. However, the complex nonlinear nature of nonlinear dynamical systems often complicates both the numerical and analytical investigation of evolutionary nonlinear dynamics, posing a significant hurdle for researchers in the field. This article aims to introduce, discuss, and establish links between established mathematical challenges and contemporary research questions within eco-evolutionary dynamics. Specifically, we present recent advancements in numerically resolving singularly perturbed nonlinear problems using the domain decomposition method paired with Hermitian deformation. Furthermore, we offer a fresh numerical perspective on and interpretation of existing results and illustrate how this technique can be effectively applied to model eco-evolutionary dynamics. The proposed approach is versatile, applicable not only to typical singularly perturbed models but also to systems characterized by slow-fast dynamics, multiple time scales, and large parameter values. We begin with a concise review of the method's theoretical underpinnings, followed by a review of recent numerical analysis of the invasion barrier within adaptive dynamics, a core mechanism driving non-linear interactions in eco-evolutionary models. Finally, we demonstrate a fundamental connection between the invasion barrier and the model's singular perturbation structure, thereby offering a fresh numerical approach to investigating evolutionarily stable strategies and periodic branching cycles. We conclude by outlining potential future research avenues within this emerging discipline. This work represents a foundational effort to integrate established methodologies from pure and applied mathematics with contemporary innovations in eco-evolutionary dynamics. By fostering connections across these disciplines, we anticipate a deeper mutual understanding, potentially yielding new insights into the intricate non-linear interactions between ecology and evolution. Our findings indicate that AMM liquidity exhibits significant asymmetry: because AMM invariant functions typically generate higher liquidity on one side of the price range for a given price movement, users favor either buying or selling, creating a demand imbalance. We demonstrate that this requirement for asymmetric liquidity results in higher transaction costs for users, as AMMs impose higher fees when moves are larger on the less-liquid side. Additionally, we illustrate how trading strategies utilizing the swap benchmark can mitigate asymmetry issues, thereby reducing costs for all market participants. the Internet of Things (IoT) has brought significant benefits, it has simultaneously introduced new challenges, including pervasive privacy and security risks. Currently, the lack of comprehensive AI/IoT security frameworks hinders widespread AI adoption within smart environments like the city. To address this gap, we introduce an extended threat model for AI/IoT systems. This model builds upon the established IoT threat model by ICECube and introduces a novel AI/IoT framework for urban planning to demonstrate the practical application of our contributions. Furthermore, the model explores the emergence of deepfakes as a consequence of merging AI and IoT, examining their practical implications through the lens of smart city applications. Our findings reveal that while AI/IoT data cannot be secured with traditional encryption methods due to privacy concerns, they can be effectively protected using a privacy-preserving scheme based on Homomorphic Encryption (HE). Additionally, our analysis identifies data leakage and data poisoning as the primary threats in AI/IoT systems, with the latter posing a more significant risk than the former. This study provides a foundational overview for future research into AI security and threats in integrated AI/IoT data environments. 80% of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) exhibit abnormal lung computer tomography (CT) findings, characterized primarily by reticulation and frequent confluent areas. **Purpose:** The objective is to evaluate whether confluent opacification on lung CT serves as a prognostic indicator for IPF patients and to assess whether automated artificial intelligence can enhance the consistency of scoring this pattern. **Methods:** Retrospective analysis was conducted on 100 IPF patients from the beginning of 2017 to determine survival rates across quartiles of confluent opacity scores obtained via a recently validated radiological scoring system. Additionally, a deep convolutional neural network (ResNet50) was trained on a dataset of 968 CTs to independently assess confluent opacification. **Results:** Higher scores for confluent opacification correlated with significantly reduced survival (p<0.001). Although automated AI scoring achieved moderate reliability compared to radiologist assessments (Pearson's r=0.52), it demonstrated a strong correlation with patient prognosis (Spearman's r=0.58). **Conclusion:** Both confluent opacification assessed by radiologists and by AI algorithms predict survival in IPF patients. While AI offers promise for quantifying this pattern, further training on diverse CT data is necessary to ensure its generalizability. **Impact:** Automated analysis of pulmonary CTs using convolutional neural networks can predict IPF patient survival. This prediction is based on extensive training with a large, annotated CT dataset, requiring no additional time or resources beyond current imaging standards. Furthermore, this method may be applied to anonymized routine clinical CTs to assist in patient risk stratification.

The analysis begins with noiseless seismic records. In this ideal scenario, seismic imaging can be achieved via the linear inversion $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a}^\dagger \mathbf{d}$, where $\mathbf{a}^\dagger$ represents the pseudo-inverse of the convolution operator defined by the blur function $\mathbf{a}$. Finally, we examine the effects of additive noise on $\mathbf{d}$, showing that the identified convex data fidelity term transforms into a regularized version incorporating the expected energy of the noise. We demonstrate that a specific class of price utilities for a seller can be identified from the demand function, provided the seller possesses additive but potentially incomplete information regarding the buyer, along with a prior probability distribution of that information to define a mean prior. The seller utilizes this prior to establish a demand function assumed to match the buyer's. Both sellers derive a price utility from their demand functions through a bargaining negotiation process. Although the price utilities generated from identical demand functions may vary depending on the seller's identity and prior probability distribution of their information, we outline methods for mitigating this discrepancy. These approaches include the seller reporting a demand function and the use of multiple iterations of bargaining negotiations. We anticipate this will serve as a foundation for further research into automated negotiation systems. To illustrate the proposed price utility generation methods, we provide a simulation using the Cournot duopoly model as a benchmark for demand functions. In our simulations, we employed the Hotelling model to represent seller demand functions and calculated the seller's price utilities through demand function generation and bargaining negotiation. We assessed the accuracy of the resulting price utilities based on the seller's identity and the number of negotiation iterations. Additionally, we computed metrics regarding the discrepancy in price utilities between two sellers to quantify the effect of seller identity on accuracy. These metrics demonstrated improved accuracy in scenarios involving reported demand functions and multiple iteration negotiations. These findings confirm the effectiveness of our approach for negotiators engaged in price bargaining. Furthermore, we demonstrated that a negotiator's identity, defined by its demand function and reported demand function, influences its price utility. We propose future research into a method for generating price utilities from demand functions based on these findings. This study represents an initial step toward creating a price negotiation support system for industrial applications, aiming to facilitate accurate and efficient negotiations between industrial partners. We believe this work will advance the goal of industrial price negotiation support systems. , there is a growing need to detect and analyze long-term trends in urban activities like traffic congestion and energy usage. However, constructing and training such models remains difficult due to their heavy reliance on expert input for defining parameters, the significant volume of data necessitating substantial storage, and the lack of generalizable frameworks for model design. This paper introduces CityLine, an architecture built on the concept of longitudinal estimation. By shifting the focus from individual sensing points to longitudinal data streams, the system achieves continuous monitoring of urban activities while minimizing the requirements for expert knowledge, storage space, and data centers. The architecture was evaluated using two real-world smart city datasets, yielding promising outcomes. CityCode, the accompanying software library, was open-sourced to facilitate the building and training of similar models. Results from these case studies demonstrate that the framework can detect varying trends in urban activities while maintaining high accuracy with a reduced need for expert knowledge. Specifically, cityView, a component of the architecture, reduces the number of parameters by up to 75% compared to other methods. Furthermore, cityLine, which enables multi-sensing analysis, achieves 90% higher F1 scores than cityView. Finally, a parameter ablation study confirms the robustness of the model across diverse city-level contexts. The findings suggest that this framework can effectively monitor urban activities using multi-sensing data, producing more stable results than alternative approaches. The complete framework is now accessible for other cities through CityLine. The study demonstrates that this approach significantly lowers the demands for expert knowledge and storage space, while city-level parameter learning allows the framework to generalize across different contexts. Specifically, inferring model parameters from sparse observations in stochastic systems presents significant difficulties, particularly when combined with measurement noise. This work addresses these issues within the framework of stochastic differential equations, proposing a Bayesian approach to estimate parameters $(\mu, \sigma)$ in the presence of measurement noise $\nu$. We adopt a uniform prior distribution $D_0(\mu, \sigma) = 1$ for simplicity, though other options exist. The posterior distribution $D_t(\mu, \neq)$ represents our updated understanding after accounting for both the stochastic differential equation and measurement noise. Typically, exact analytical solutions for $D_t$ are unattainable; therefore, we approximate it using an ensemble of parameters $\{(\mu_i, \sigma_i)\}_i$ generated via an importance sampling importance reweighting procedure. This method allows the posterior to be represented as a distribution over parameters, enabling the calculation of moments and moments. We validate this approach using the Lorenz equations, where parameter estimation is attempted with noisy and incomplete data. Additionally, we provide an overview of parameter estimation without measurement noise for systems of stochastic differential equations. Finally, a Python implementation of this methodology is available at https://github.com/CMacArthur-2020/ParameterEstimation. Our results demonstrate that this technique offers a efficient and effective framework for estimating parameters from sparse, noisy data in stochastic systems. These findings have broad implications for any scientific domain utilizing continuous-time stochastic models to describe complex, noisy data. Specifically, this approach is highly valuable in experimental sciences where parameter inference is required despite noisy and incomplete measurements. Furthermore, this methodology complements recent advances in data-driven stochastic modeling that utilize ensemble-based data assimilation to constrain parameters. We anticipate that these techniques will enhance the accuracy of ensemble-based data assimilation methods. Furthermore, the employed importance sampling importance reweighting procedure can be independently applied to analyze ensembles generated by MCMC, variational Bayesian, or stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods. By determining the optimal acceptance rate and proposing a fixed-step-size Leapfrog integrator, we achieve faster convergence for large-scale parameter estimation, making our algorithm scalable to high-dimensional parameter spaces. These features address a significant limitation in ensemble-based data assimilation, thereby enhancing the reliability of parameter inference and model selection. We believe this methodology will significantly benefit research across all fields utilizing continuous-time stochastic models, provided measurements are available. Despite these gains, deep learning models often exhibit reduced generalization when encountering domain shifts during testing, leading to substantial declines in diagnostic performance. While one-hot encoding has been standard for encoding DNA sequences, we demonstrate that pretraining an autoencoder on this format significantly enhances the accuracy of genomic variant detection compared to architectures lacking such components. Additionally, we find that both recurrent and convolutional networks achieve comparable performance, yet we illustrate that the recent use of Transformer-based models for this task was overly complicated. As an end-to-end approach, our top-performing model achieves an AUC of 0.9229 on the IMPC dataset and 0.8906 on the Decaplex dataset. Furthermore, we show that these models effectively identify variants within previously unseen samples. We make the source code and pretrained models accessible at https://github.com/jeremymcalmon/GenomicVariantDetection. To validate the utility of these models for downstream applications, we evaluated their performance in identifying genes associated with specific phenotypes using gene set statistics and pathway analysis. Our results indicate that existing tools are insufficient for this purpose; consequently, we propose a new tool, PhenoMatch, available at https://github.com/jeremymcalom/PhenoMatch. We anticipate that this integrated approach will facilitate the use of deep learning in downstream analyses to identify genes and biological pathways linked to specific phenotypes. Finally, we discuss how this strategy adheres to the principles of interpretable machine learning and offers strategies to enhance model interpretability. Given that genomic variant detection is inherently an interpretability challenge, we demonstrate how identifying local features and motifs contributes to making deep learning models more transparent. Ultimately, we conclude that deep learning holds great promise for downstream applications, paving the way for specific future research directions. These insights aim to inspire researchers to uncover new applications for deep learning in genomics. Furthermore, we demonstrate a general procedure for constructing a time-dependent generalized coordinate transformation that simplifies the equations of motion for multi-dimensional partially integrable systems into this new canonical format. This approach yields significant direct and indirect applications for both analytic and numerical simulations of multi-dimensional partially integrable systems. Specifically, in the direct application, we show that while the standard method by Mikkelsen and Moldauer requires representation structures to be preserved over extended times only near the initial moment, our new transformation maintains this structure accurately both structurally and numerically for all time. For the indirect application, we demonstrate that frequency components can be computed directly and accurately from the transformed equations of motion without solving the system numerically. Consequently, this enables high-precision evaluation of long-time dynamical properties and the construction of long-time valid quasi-analytic models. We provide a detailed physical example using the example under consideration. Additionally, our representation structures facilitate the design of efficient long-time numerical integrators for multi-dimensional partially integrable systems and serve as a substantial foundation for investigating and analyzing various numerical properties and schemes. Finally, we present a strategy for incorporating our new structure-preserving transformation and algorithm into existing symplectic or energy-conserving integrators to achieve even better numerical performance. We present a detailed example of a 3D partially integrable model to illustrate the physical and numerical implications. Overall, our framework offers immense potential for advancing the theoretical understanding and practical computation of multi-dimensional partially integrable systems. In a forthcoming companion paper, we will explore more general structure-preserving transformation structures and their applications. Meanwhile, in an accompanying numerical paper, we will systematically validate the structural and physical advantages of our structure-preserving transformation and algorithm using the 3D partially integrable model as an example. These structure-preserving structures are also forming the basis for future extensions to address more complex problems, such as multi-dimensional partially integrable systems with slow-fast structures.
