employed metrics for evaluating how closely two time series resemble one another. However, it fails to capture certain types of dissimilarity, including specific distributional variations and temporal misalignments. To address these limitations, we introduce the Pearson Distance, a metric designed to measure temporal misalignment and other form-based dissimilarities between time series. This distance function satisfies the axioms of a metric space and serves as a special case of a broader class of Pearson distances that accept any real-valued weighting of the temporal axis. Computationally, it can be achieved by extending the classical algorithm, resulting in only a linear increase in runtime relative to the time series length. Empirical evaluations across various synthetic datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. Additionally, we present a novel synthetic dataset, Synchronized Series (SS), which enables a comprehensive examination of the conditions under which different Pearson Distances are most effective. Our empirical study reveals that, contingent upon the specific characteristics of the input data, a Pearson Distance can outperform other correlation metrics, such as Dynamic Time Warping. Finally, we explore the utility of a newly defined conceptual space concerning the parameters of a Pearson Distance. Empirical analyses within this space identify subsets of parameters suited for specific synchronization tasks. These contributions facilitate the selection of an appropriate Pearson Distance for any given problem context. The source code and the new dataset are available at https://github.com/CTransformLab/PearsonDistance. Supplementary materials can be found at https://doi.org/10.7910/D0Q94R. Both repositories are licensed under CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0. To our knowledge, this research represents a first step toward a principled selection of a specific Pearson Distance. Furthermore, the application of a new conceptual space concept, which is a fundamental component of this work, has not been previously explored. We anticipate that these contributions will advance both Time Series Analysis and Visual Analysis research. Furthermore, we believe that a metric space concept is of significant interest to the broader Computer Science community. This work is derived from a presentation at the 34th ACM SIGSPATIAL International Conference (2026). Specifically, it addresses the challenge that, despite the availability of multiple correlation-based dissimilarity measures, no principled selection criteria exist for real-world applications. Our research demonstrates that, dependent on specific task characteristics, a Pearson Distance can effectively solve this problem. This study systematically examines how superconducting gap anisotropy influences the current-voltage characteristics of a hybrid nanoconstriction. By combining $k \cdot p$-theory with the quasiclassical Green's function framework, we calculate the anisotropy of the superconducting order parameter within the semiconductor channel. Our findings indicate that, anisotropy aside, tunneling processes yield approximately identical thermal conductance and quasiparticle density of states across all voltage biases. However, regarding topological quasiparticles, we observe that right-moving modes remain nodeless anisotropy-free zero-energy states within the normal regime but acquire an energy gap anisotropy-dependent away from zero bias. Additionally, we introduce a concept for the transmittance anisotropy-dependent quasiparticle density of states and calculate the topological quasiparticle density based on this density matrix element. Finally, we demonstrate how to distinguish between transmittance anisotropy effects and deviations from the $d$-wave model in the quasiparticle density of states. These results provide a foundation for analyzing anisotropic superconducting gaps anisotropy-independent in future experiments involving superconducting-semiconducting nanoconstrictions. This study investigates stars with masses of 0.5 and 2.0 solar masses (M$_\odot$) during the key accretion and pre-planetary stages of stellar evolution, utilizing advanced radiative transfer codes alongside updated stellar evolution models, disk chemistry, and planet formation theories. We examine XUV flux levels and their impact on disk evolution, carbon monoxide (CO) depletion, and the location of the "snowline," which marks the inner edge of the CO ice-rich region crucial for planet formation. Our findings indicate that CO snowlines in these disks are, on average, approximately 30 astronomical units (AU) closer to the central star compared to what is observed in present-day disks, such as those in the Orion Nebula. Additionally, CO is significantly depleted within the inner 100 AU of both low- and high-mass disk models, though coagulation processes may help preserve some CO. The resulting CO distributions shape the initial conditions for planet formation, including the stability of planetary orbits and the migration of planetary cores and ices. Furthermore, the high XUV fluxes predicted for young stars may accelerate the dissipation of protoplanetary disks, with gas depletion occurring approximately 10 million years (Myr) sooner than dust. This implies that the window for core formation and migration to final orbits is much shorter than previously thought. Finally, the intense XUV flux may trigger further water ice depletion in disk outer regions, potentially explaining the scarcity of ice-rich objects beyond the snowline in our own solar system and others. In conclusion, the environment provided by young stars and their disks offers a distinct phase for planet formation, with high XUV fluxes and varying snowline positions playing pivotal roles. These results will be compared with emerging observational data from ALMA and the James Webb Space Telescope. To derive radiation friction, we analyze how radiation radiation affects the renormalization of the worldline action's expansion coefficients. Although this approach maintains the essence of the radiation friction term from the classical Lindhard-Lephtler equation, physically significant modifications arise due to alterations in the point particle's electromagnetic field. These changes are consistently described by a generalized radiative Landau-Lifshitz-Dixon equation. We explicitly calculate the contributions of both real and virtual photons to the radiative terms in this equation across three distinct curved vacuum backgrounds: de Sitter space, anti-de Sitter space, and Einstein-MacDonald two-spheres. In each case, we demonstrate that radiative acceleration is driven by the curvature of the background spacetime. Additionally, in scenarios lacking a preferred time coordinate, we show that a consistent definition of radiation friction requires modifying the Landau-Lifshitz-Dixon force to incorporate the spacetime Killing energy. We argue that this revised definition of radiative acceleration for highly radiating point charges in curved spacetimes is an essential component of a comprehensive quantum theory of particle radiation and radiation reaction. Finally, we outline an effective degrees of freedom methodology to bridge the gap between worldline quantum field theory and quantum general relativity. Although network science has long recognized and investigated emergent networks that combine multiple metrics to represent multifaceted interactions, graph neural networks (GNNs) have predominantly focused on learning from a single metric or representation. To address limitations in capturing emerging features or representing interactions from various perspectives, graph transformers have recently emerged as a method for multi-graph learning. However, current approaches typically require pre-specifying emergent features or lack flexibility in adapting to different interactions. We introduce GGNN, a framework that learns graph representations by integrating networks built from different attributes while simultaneously inferring graph features. Specifically, GGNN constructs individual networks using distinct attributes to capture emerging interactions, then employs generalized attention to adaptively learn representations by leveraging cross-graph correlations to infer missing network constructions. We validate GGNN's effectiveness on real-world datasets across node classification, link prediction, and single-graph classification tasks. Additionally, we ablate the generalized attention mechanism to demonstrate its capacity to select pertinent pre-identified graph architectures for representation learning. Finally, we multi-graph ablate the framework to highlight the benefits of inferring both pre-identified and unobserved network topologies. These results underscore GGNN's potential in representing complex interactions and inferring unobserved networks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/kevinzhang97/GGNN. This work examines the molecular origins of such phenomena by employing molecular dynamics simulations to analyze the behavior of liquid argon near a solid argon surface. The simulations utilize a thin film of liquid argon with periodic boundary conditions in the plane parallel to the solid surface. Our results indicate that local molecular ordering influences the effective contact angle, while the intrinsic contact angle remains governed by the frequency of hydrogen bonds in the interfacial regions. Furthermore, simulations with varying solid argon lattice orientations relative to the liquid reveal diverse local ordering patterns, which subsequently affect the effective orientation of the interfacial molecules. Overall, these findings provide insights into the molecular mechanisms driving liquid-liquid-solid interactions. By introducing metrics in both Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks, we prove Lipschitz stability for these respective metrics. The findings for the Eulerian case represent an improvement upon previous work addressing the case where $\alpha=0$. Additionally, we examine the limits of these results by demonstrating that Lipschitz stability generally fails for general (non-constant) $\alpha$-dissipative energies. Finally, we analyze the behavior of the solution at finite-time blow-up, noting that while the Lagrangian metric becomes singular, remainders remain bounded provided $\alpha \ge 1/2$. Specifically, when $\alpha=1/2$, the solution exhibits optimal Lipschitz regularity, aligning with established literature on the point blow-up solution to the Hunter-Saxton equation. Furthermore, we extend these metrics to solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation subject to general boundary conditions. Although the solutions lack optimal regularity a priori, we establish that they maintain Lipschitz stability in the modified metrics. Specifically, we confirm that the results from [15] regarding the stability of the singular traveling wave solution are encompassed within our framework. Moreover, we demonstrate that this framework offers a more intuitive and straightforward derivation of the findings in [15] compared to the original methodology. Moreover, we demonstrate that our framework can yield new insights into the stability of the said traveling wave. Finally, we extend the results from [15] to a broader class of traveling wave solutions, all of which display optimal Lipschitz regularity. These newly identified solutions feature non-constant profiles and distinct behaviors at spatial infinity. As a supplementary contribution, we also prove the existence of these solutions. Such extensions were previously unaddressed in the literature. These discoveries arise from applying our current framework, offering both an advantage and a limitation relative to earlier methods. From one perspective, our framework facilitates the discovery of these new solutions; from another, it restricts the applicability of these metrics to only those solutions possessing Lipschitz regularity. These metrics find significant utility in analyzing the convergence of various regularizations, including smooth approximations and vortex-sheet approximations. In this context, we apply our framework to provide a streamlined and precise proof of the convergence of vortex-sheet approximations toward $\alpha$-dissipative solutions. This scarcity of high-quality views hinders the accurate and robust classification of lung pathologies. This study presents a deep learning approach designed to automatically generate and select high-quality views for lung image analysis.

**Methods:** We adapted a widely used data augmentation technique—BasicAutoConvexConvex—by incorporating it as a specialized component within a new architecture named TransConvexConvex. This method iteratively selects and generates images while selecting views to extract representative features. It achieves this by utilizing both feature-level representations and original images as inputs to guide the selection of high-quality images. The model employs a U-net-based segmentation network to identify scan planes and selects characteristic images based on tissue-like characteristics using ResNet50. Finally, feature similarity is calculated at the image level to choose highly representative images for training a multi-classifier.

**Results:** The proposed model achieved an accuracy of approximately 80% with an AUC of 0.85 across 11 lung diseases, significantly surpassing results from baseline models featuring basic or widely adopted augmentation strategies. Furthermore, a radiologist confirmed that the views generated and selected by our model are superior to those routinely chosen by experienced sonographers.

**Conclusions:** This research introduces an advanced machine learning model for lung ultrasound view generation. The primary innovation lies in linking view-based features with view-independent image representations during representation learning to simultaneously guide view generation and selection. This allows the model to produce views with distinctive tissue characteristics and select images that best represent the underlying class, leading to highly accurate lung disease classification. By linking view quality to specific tissue characteristics, our model offers a more interpretable alternative to current black-box deep learning methods. This approach demonstrates significant potential for enhancing the diagnosis of lung diseases. Additionally, the model is well-suited for adaptation to other ultrasound-based medical image classification tasks. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhongyikevin/LUNA-USViewGen. This paper introduces a novel approach to entity classification within texts containing instances of sexual harassment—a specific subset of hate speech. By leveraging emergent learning, our method integrates data from multiple, often isolated, domains knowledgeably. We demonstrate that this approach effectively categorizes entities that are implicated, present, or affected by sexual harassment, even when explicitly denied in contexts where such acts are framed as jokes. Building on the hypothesis that human readers implicitly analyze local contextual information to understand specific entities in these texts, we developed two models: one based on rule induction and another utilizing memory networks. Both models exhibit performance comparable to that achieved by human readers. When applied to the Large-scale Semi-Supervised Learning for Distant Supervision (LSSD) dataset, which focuses on online sexual harassment, our method accurately classifies entities that are clearly involved in harassment cases as well as those where the harassment is subtly implied. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of narrative analysis within hate speech research. Nevertheless, these designs frequently encounter issues such as non-uniform component variations, manufacturing inconsistencies, and software bugs, leading to faulty activity in specific components. These defects result in sub-optimal MIMO performance, including imbalanced computational loads, diminished throughput, increased latency, and elevated energy consumption. We introduce REBAL, a framework comprising REweighting and EXcluding strategies to restore MIMO functionality by dynamically reconfiguring execution across redundant units. Specifically, REbal re-weights execution weight values and re-partitions the MIMO array by either excluding defective components or ignoring their contributions to the MIMO sum. We present two main rebalancing techniques: (i) REweight, which re-distributes the MIMO sum by adjusting the execution weight of each unit, and (ii) EXcl, which re-distributes the sum by excluding or including redundant units that are either partially or fully active or inactive. Comprehensive evaluations across various MIMO architectures with diverse defect types demonstrate that REbal can restore performance to near-optimal levels. Notably, REbal outperforms naive exclusion by up to 1.96x (average 1.33x) in latency and energy efficiency. Furthermore, REbal can restore within-spec MIMO performance to average above-spec requirements in failed designs, facilitating their adoption in time- or energy-constrained environments. Finally, REbal delivers an average of 1.26x latency and 1.36x energy efficiency gains compared to rebalanced MIMO competitors across a broad spectrum of designs with differing MIMO counts and defect levels. The rebalancing overhead is minimal, consuming only 0.5% to 3.5% of execution time. Our results indicate that REbal can recover the average above-spec MIMO design's performance to meet the original target specifications, without incurring any rebalancing overhead. Additionally, REbal can restore the performance of failed MIMO designs to satisfy the time-energy constraints of up to 20000 smaller designs with reduced latency. The rebalancing overhead remains negligible for both above-spec and failed MIMO designs, and REbal effectively restores the performance of failed designs to compete with above-spec MIMO architectures. This study introduces a new quantification metric for CKD and establishes a multistate model that accounts for individual heterogeneity, low exposure levels, and measurement errors. The proposed statistical model quantifies the cumulative exposure to a risk factor across the life course by integrating data from multiple time points. Applied to a rheumatoid arthritis (RA) dataset, the findings reveal a strong multistate pattern: RA patients exhibit a higher prevalence of CKD at younger ages compared to non-RA individuals, with this difference widening over time. This method is broadly adaptable to various conditions affecting the general population where multiple time-point assessments are available. It offers enhanced understanding of the pathways leading to CKD, thereby facilitating targeted, timely, and cost-effective interventions to mitigate risk progression and alleviate the disease's burden. These results may also assist clinicians in identifying high-risk patients and understanding patient trajectories more effectively than current diagnostic tools allow, ultimately improving treatment strategies. Finally, the study includes a simulation demonstrating the model's robustness under conditions of high within-subject variability and measurement error. The findings indicate that this approach is well-suited for analyzing CKD progression within the life course epidemiology framework. We anticipate that this method will prove valuable in future investigations into CKD pathways using general population data, such as national health examinations. It will support the development of prevention strategies, including risk prediction models and high-risk patient identification, by elucidating the mechanisms underlying CKD progression. intervals, known as hothouse states, caused by changes in the carbon-silicon cycle, such as CO2 and SiC burial. While these events, including hothouses, cool states (snowballs), and hothouse-to-snowball transitions, are often modeled using simplified energy balance models, this study incorporates both the ice-albedo and silicate weathering feedbacks into a one-dimensional climate model. The results reveal that the hothouse state is actually a tri-stable state, coexisting with two snowball states. This finding offers a deeper understanding of Earth's potential hothouse and snowball configurations and highlights significant implications for exoplanets, some of which may maintain only hothouse or snowball conditions. For specific exoplanets, even minor variations in stellar insolation could trigger abrupt, planet-wide transitions between hothouse and snowball states, a phenomenon termed an exo-Milankovitch hysteresis event. This type of feedback loop could drastically alter habitability by limiting liquid water availability and/or sequestering essential nutrients in ice and snow. Consequently, such exo-Milankovitch hysteresis events should be considered when assessing the habitability of Hadean and Archean Earth, as well as of exoplanets. Given that tidal forces may be stronger around smaller, cooler, or more massive stars, hothouse and snowball states could be more prevalent in planetary systems orbiting such stars. Consequently, the exo-Milankovitch hysteresis effect and the presence of exoplanetary hothouses and snowoballs should be part of future habitability studies.

Nevertheless, they suffer from poor generalization when faced with distribution shifts in out-of-domain (OOD) data, a significant challenge given the vast diversity of clinical settings, such as variations in image acquisition protocols, patient demographics, and scanner types. This study presents a novel three-stage transfer learning framework that enhances cross-domain robustness for medical image segmentation tasks.

**Method:** We begin with large-scale pre-training on a generic domain, followed by a coarse-to-fine instance selection strategy on limited target domain data. Finally, a self-supervised contrastive loss function optimizes feature representations in latent space. This training process is maintained while executing the outer-inner optimization typical of pseudo-labeling techniques. Specifically, during the inner loop, we select target instances based on a novel threshold-based selection strategy that filters for instances with high pseudo-label scores and robust features. In the outer loop, we leverage these selected instances to refine network parameters, thereby minimizing a contrastive loss designed to boost cross-domain feature representation. This approach promises greater generalization for OOD data, addressing distribution shifts through enhanced invariance.

**Results:** We evaluated the method on multi-modality segmentation of abdominal organs using MASS-pretrained V-Net models. Cross-validation yielded a Dice score of 85.96%, representing a 4.76% increase compared to standard V-Net results. Furthermore, the proposed approach surpasses recent state-of-the-art methods, such as Mean-Std Entropy Minimization (MS-ENT) and Virtual Domain Adversarial Network (ViDaN).

**Conclusion:** Our method effectively addresses the challenge of domain shift by learning target domain samples in feature space. These selected instances possess more discriminative features, are better aligned, and exhibit higher certainty, all of which contribute to improved OOD generalization. Additionally, the proposed method is not restricted to specific pre-training strategies or selection criteria, offering broad applicability in similar contexts. **Code:** https://github.com/zhaojiaqi-git/MedSegNet_PCL.

The model derives a new transport equation for an eddy viscosity matrix defined over a hierarchy of Reynolds stresses. This event occurred approximately 25,000 to 30,000 years ago, with SGRAE being generally accepted as a single galactic supernova remnant. a supergravity unified framework serves as a viable dark matter candidate. This scenario emerges in a hidden sector with minimal or no interactions with the visible sector, where dark matter decays are governed exclusively by gravity. We propose a specific model involving a two-sector structure under a unified $SU(5)\times U(1)_X$ symmetry, which incorporates a non-Abelian global symmetry across both sectors. In this configuration, the LSP in the visible sector is primarily the gravitino, while the LSP in the hidden sector is the neutralino $\psi$. Assuming a near-uniform dark matter distribution, we show that a significant portion of the gravitino dark matter can be produced via the decay of the hidden sector LSP. We derive a lower limit for the mass of the heavy LSP based on X-boson exchange between the hidden and visible sectors and calculate the abundance of gravitino dark matter resulting from this decay. Our analysis indicates that for LSP masses ranging from $10^{11}$ GeV to $10^{14}$ GeV, the exchange of an X-boson with masses between $10^{12}$ GeV and $10^{17}$ GeV can generate sufficient gravitino abundance to account for all observed dark matter, even in scenarios where primordial primordial gravitino production is suppressed. We estimate that the abundance of gravitino dark matter generated by this LSP decay could constitute between 1% and 100% of the total dark matter density, depending on the specific LSP mass. Furthermore, we examine the current experimental status regarding spin-1/2 to spin-1/2 decay within this scenario and present limits on the LSP mass derived from existing experimental constraints. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting such decaying LSPs through indirect signals in the cosmic ray electron and gamma-ray spectra. We demonstrate that LSP decays within this proposed model generate characteristic spectral distortions in high-energy electron and gamma-ray fluxes, offering a promising new avenue for experimental verification. This research expands upon our previous work [arXiv:1709.09144 [hep-ph]] by specifically addressing supergravity frameworks. Additionally, we have incorporated several new references and incorporated minor updates to address certain issues present in our prior publication. [Preliminary version. The objective of this study is to create a system capable of anticipating events ahead of time, specifically targeting incidents that compromise a driver's cognitive state and impair their driving capabilities. To achieve this, driver state data was collected using a head-mounted, multi-sensory sensor fusion device that tracks both visual and auditory inputs. Furthermore, current learning algorithms typically assume access to fully observed fields, rendering them ineffective for practical scenarios involving missing data. Although it is established that randomly generated graphs are largely leaf-sensitive, we demonstrate that the cycle $C_n$ serves as the sole minimax graph that is not leaf-sensitive, thereby resolving a long-standing conjecture. Furthermore, we examine other minimax structures, specifically complete bipartite graphs, and propose several conjectures regarding their sensitivity profiles. Additionally, we characterize the graph class possessing uniquely maximal minimax sets and provide an efficient algorithm for constructing them. Our analysis reveals that all examined classes are indeed leaf-sensitive, contrasting with the distinct properties of maximax sets, whose sensitive structures are significantly more complex. Leveraging current findings, we introduce a novel approach for computing the full set of maximum independent sets. This method utilizes the graph's sensitivity type—whether it is tree-like, bipartite, or neither—as a threshold: if leaf sensitivity exists, we enumerate independent sets below the relevant count to generate the target set; otherwise, we employ a recursive backtracking algorithm. Although the first approach carries higher time complexity, it is substantially more efficient than backtracking for graphs with many branch vertices. Consequently, we construct a new independent set generator that capitalizes on these structural properties. Experimental outcomes indicate that our algorithm is approximately 100 times faster than the implementation in the leading open-source graph library (NetworkX). By integrating this algorithm with Picard-Landau duality, we develop an efficient method for counting non-isomorphic maximal independent sets. Finally, we investigate the joint probability distribution of the independent number and maximum packing number within the class of forests, deriving exact results for specific forest types and asymptotic formulas for random forests. Monte-Carlo simulations confirm the validity of these theoretical developments. Furthermore, we introduce a novel, surprisingly complex formula for the exact mean of maximum independent sets in forests, validated through simulation. All accompanying programs are available in the IGraph Library. Our results suggest that the sensitive nature of maximum independent sets in forests is crucial for the efficiency of our algorithms. Leveraging this, we explore the potential application of the sensitive maximax set algorithm for maximax set generation. Given the sensitive structure of bipartite graphs, our algorithm outperforms existing methods for graphs up to 150 vertices, as verified through simulation. By directly comparing experimental results with directed and directed$\;$+$\;$nondirected flow components modeled using hydrodynamics, we derive constraints regarding the equation of state governing the hot, dense nuclear matter produced. Specifically, we demonstrate that the nondirected flow component is highly sensitive to the nonstrange equation of state within the mid-rapidity zone, as well as to the initial spatial anisotropy of the collision system. These findings explicitly rule out any softening of the nonstrange equation of state at low energy densities associated with the nuclear matter phase transition, a scenario previously suggested by some analyses. This "frustrated" mode arises from the interference between the central system's real and imaginary interaction components. It possesses lower frequencies than any individual interaction term, scales as the square root of $N$ (where $N$ is the bath size), and markedly alters the large frequency tail of the system's spectrum. This behavior is illustrated using an extended Hubbard model involving spin-orbit coupled fermions or a phase-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric driven-dissipative quantum optics model featuring complex nonlinearities. We outline that this non-Gaussian nature can be utilized to certify the presence of complex interactions. We conclude by suggesting that the entanglement produced by an unstable frustrated mode offers a distinct advantage over other entanglement sources due to its non-Gaussian character. Extending this principle to soft robotic systems—which display dynamic deformations absent in static chiral structures—could yield new locomotion strategies and deformation patterns. This study demonstrates for the first time the integration of material geometrical chirality with actuation to achieve a soft robot's three-dimensional locomotion. To accomplish this, we created a soft robot with intrinsic chiral deformation governed by its design geometry rather than external forces. We utilized the soft printing technique to accurately introduce chiral features, achieving designs with well-defined handedness and orientation. Following the development of this chiral architecture, we engineered locomotor behaviors including C-shaped twisting, helical twisting, and bending. The synergy between material softness and geometrical chirality produces novel, efficient locomotion strategies that remain impossible with purely rigid chiral structures. Consequently, mastering the interaction between softness and chirality represents a vital direction for advancing soft robotics. This research not only deepens our comprehension of chiral design and chiral locomotion in soft robotics but also establishes a new paradigm for the field's future progress.

To achieve a rigorous comparison, we explicitly derive the energy spectrum for a single fermion confined by the potential of both theories, employing appropriate spin structures. We demonstrate that despite minor differences arising from the discretization of the area, the energy spectra of the fermions are identical. This finding underscores that the previously reported equivalence between JT gravity and T2D remains valid within the path integral formulation. Additionally, we provide insights into the equivalence between JT gravity and dilaton gravity when converted to the canonical formulation. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for black hole modeling and the semi-classical derivation of the black hole information paradox. We explicitly calculate the one-point correlation function of a scalar field as a function of the dilaton field, modeling it as describing particle creation near a horizon. Utilizing these correlation functions, we estimate the rate of entanglement entropy growth for a quantum field interacting with a black hole. Furthermore, we examine the relationship of this growth rate with the Penrose process. Although the outcome is not entirely positive, this approach offers a viable path to advancing the investigation of the paradox associated with black hole evaporation. We also explore several avenues for future research. In our effort to bridge the two theories, we provide explicit evidence supporting the hypothesis that relevant research in the quantum gravity regime must extend beyond the semi-classical approximation. These results, derived within a path integral framework, offer alternative perspectives compared to those obtained via canonical methods. Our research demonstrates that the established equivalence between JT gravity and T2D can be derived without relying on heuristic methods. By employing a more explicit calculation technique, we believe these findings will serve as a valuable reference for future studies. We hope this work contributes to deepening understanding in this exciting area of inquiry. (We thank Chien-Yu S. Chu and Ching-Hsiang Lee for their comments on this work. This study applies the Schwarzschild metric to model the formation and collapse of such a bubble, thereby creating a black hole within this framework. We show that as the bubble velocity approaches the speed of light relative to the surrounding space, a black hole forms and collapses asymptotically. Further analysis of this collapsed state yields the Hoop Conjecture and a concept akin to gravitational lensing. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the resulting object is not a traditional Schwarzschild black hole, as general relativistic effects—specifically, the presence of (super)massive stars—prevent the formation of a standard event horizon. However, constructing new pipelines in urban areas is difficult due to space constraints and the risk of damaging adjacent utilities. Tunnelless microtunneling offers a promising solution for creating new pipelines in constrained urban environments, yet current methods often struggle with alignment accuracy, especially when navigating curved sections. Tiny, agile robots could overcome these limitations, but manually guiding them presents significant challenges. This paper introduces a novel control mechanism that enables a team of small robots to self-organize and navigate the tunnel in a coordinated sequence. When positioned at the tunnel's leading edge, this control law maintains alignment along the path and keeps robots evenly spaced. Furthermore, a new adjustment control allows robots ahead of the target line to slow down or pause, while those behind are attracted to advance. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through 2D numerical simulations of various scenarios, as well as experimental validation using real robots in a physical tunnel. These results confirm the approach works effectively for both straight and curved tunnel navigation. Furthermore, the experiments indicate that hardware issues, such as wheel slippage, actually enhance robustness against disturbances rather than reducing it. Finally, the study shows that a team of six robots can execute the migration from the entry to the exit of both straight and curved tunnels within three minutes. This research paves the way for applying microtunneling techniques to small, unmanned systems, ultimately aiding in the analysis and automation of tunnel construction and maintenance. Although numerous theories attempt to explain this phenomenon, this study proposes a fresh perspective by framing the problem within a "multiple-timescale learning" framework. By analyzing a simple two-armed bandit scenario, we demonstrate that as the learning rate on the slower timescale decreases, the learning dynamics converge to either a maximization or a probability-matching strategy, contingent upon the exploration approach used. Specifically, the standard "average-utility" exploration mechanism drives the learner toward maximization, whereas the "state" average-utility approach results in probability-matching. This finding suggests that both process and value uncertainty must be accounted for to fully explain why both strategies persist in natural environments. Furthermore, we illustrate the potential application of this theoretical framework to biological systems. We contend that the multiple-timescale learning mechanism, which integrates both probabilistic learning and reinforcement learning principles, accurately accounts for the behavior of both healthy and autistic children engaged in probabilistic learning tasks. Consequently, our findings may offer a pathway to elucidating the learning mechanisms inherent in the human brain. Additionally, we show that the learning parameters derived from human experimental data align with those observed in both animals and robots navigating similar decision-making challenges. Specifically, the objective is to develop a polylog(n)-space algorithm capable of identifying a "near neighbor" for a given query $q$ within an input set $P$, provided such an element exists at a distance $\delta n$ from $P$. If no such element exists, the algorithm must return a candidate $p'$ where a near neighbor of $q$ within distance $\delta n$ is not found. We introduce a randomized algorithm operating in $O(mn^\epsilon)$ time and $O(\epsilon^{-1}\log^2 n)$ space. By optimizing the value of $\epsilon$, we demonstrate that for any $\epsilon > 0$, an algorithm can solve the $((1+\epsilon)\sqrt{n}/\log n)$-approximate near neighbor problem in $O(m^\epsilon n)$ time using $O(\epsilon^{-1}\log^2 n)$ space. Additionally, we present a variant of this algorithm with $O(\epsilon^{-1}\log n)$ space requiring $O(m^\epsilon n (\log\log n)^{2\epsilon})$ time. These findings offer alternative proofs for the exact near neighbor problem (when $\epsilon=0$) previously established by Indyk and Smolensky and by Seshadhri et al. in 2007. Furthermore, for $\epsilon > 0$, our approach surpasses the parameters of the best prior algorithm proposed by Chen et al. in 2009.

In separate work, Alon et al. introduced the concept of $\tau$-error hash families to address the set disjointness problem in the randomized communication complexity model. Using this framework, they achieved a $\tau$-approximate set disjointness problem solvable in $O(\tau^2/\epsilon^2)\log n$ time with a $\tau$-hash family of size $O(\epsilon^{-1}\log n)$. In this paper, we demonstrate a significant improvement over the $\tau$-hash families employed by Alon et al. For every $\epsilon > 0$, we present a $\tau$-hash family with a sufficient number of hashes such that the $\tau$-approximate set disjointness problem can be solved with $O(\epsilon^{-1}\log n)$ queries with high probability. This represents an exponential enhancement compared to the hash parameters required by Alon et al. for the same task.

Existing MEM strategies encounter a dilemma: techniques that scale effectively with qubit count often produce negative probabilities, whereas those ensuring a valid probability distribution lack scalability. We contrast out-of-plane and in-plane configurations by analyzing the objective images formed in the opposite gap space under these conditions. By solving two distinct models of a nonlocal and spill-out-out-of-plane objective—using an objective function derived from electron density—to image the gap region between two silver semi-infinite slabs, we compute the image within each nonlocal objective by integrating the product of the object and the point-to-point impulse response. Our results reveal that nonlocal effects consistently cause image broadening and darken the background in both configurations. However, the out-of-plane objective yields a smaller field of view, is more sensitive to the image formation distance, and produces a more pronounced spill-out effect, all of which reduce image quality compared to the in-out-of-plane objective. Furthermore, these out-of-plane effects become increasingly significant in the strong nonlocal regime. We also observe that the objective image is highly dependent on the choice of coordinate origin, emphasizing the necessity of carefully originating the coordinate system. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that incorporating nonlocal and spill-out effects can enable the design of novel and optimized plasmonic nanoscale imaging and superlensing systems.

Addressing the issue that objective functions originally designed for glasses may not be entirely suitable for plasmonics, this paper addresses two specific problems: the selection of an appropriate objective function and the determination of the coordinate origin. We begin by analyzing out-of-plane and in-plane objective functions to image the gap between two metallic slabs, comparing the resulting images to assess their efficacy. By observing image backgrounds and fields of view, we determine a more suitable coordinate origin and evaluate the appropriateness of each objective function. Additionally, we investigate the physical meaning behind these objective functions and propose an optimized configuration, demonstrating its superior image quality. These findings offer a foundation for future optimization of such objectives.

To further enhance image quality, we explore the potential of introducing a capping dielectric layer on the metallic region. By calculating the objective image for this new configuration, we confirm its ability to improve image results. Collectively, these findings indicate that integrating nonlocality and spillout effects can generate efficient and optimized plasmonic nanoscale imaging and superlensing systems.

A primary strategy to address data scarcity involves transferring knowledge between tasks, with data augmentation representing a particularly simple transfer learning technique. Despite its simplicity, augmentation often yields a disproportionately large performance gain relative to its engineering investment. This study aims to identify methods for enhancing performance through practical augmentation without incurring the high costs associated with complex approaches. We evaluate the effectiveness of augmentation across three independent datasets (MS-MRI, DeepLesion, and ICMLAR-2020) using four common techniques, three advanced methods, and three baseline models, which together form a total of 138 experimental scenarios. These experiments allow for a detailed analysis of how augmentation impacts performance across different contexts, including the correlation between training augmented data and performance improvements, the effects of overfitting, and the influence of specific techniques, methods, and tasks. Our findings indicate that simple augmentation strategies can be as effective, or even superior, to complex ones for MS lesion segmentation, with the optimal technique varying based on the specific task, existing prior knowledge, and target domain. Ultimately, we demonstrate that simple methods for generating synthetic data are highly effective for MS lesion segmentation, helping to mitigate the limitations of limited data in a heterogeneous testing environment. Although deep learning approaches have demonstrated remarkable success in predicting dynamics, assessing their performance remains difficult due to the absence of a unified metric and the variability in data availability. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to establish performance bounds that quantify how close a model's dynamics are to the true system by evaluating its data fidelity. We utilize these bounds to evaluate predictive capabilities based on available data and to benchmark different data-driven techniques. To derive the bounds, we evaluate two methodologies: one that minimizes the difference between model outputs and ground truth, and another that directly compares the model dynamics with the true system dynamics. To enhance estimation, we propose two strategies for generating training data via system simulations. Furthermore, we experimentally compare these methodologies and data generation approaches across various data-driven schemes, including recurrent neural networks, neural ordinary differential equations, and ensemble Kalman filters. We estimate and verify the performance bounds on a system where exact bounds are known to validate their accuracy in both identification and approximation scenarios. Finally, we demonstrate how these bounds serve to measure the performance of diverse schemes and generate sets. To ensure reproducibility, the source code is made publicly accessible. To our knowledge, this represents the first formulation of performance bounds for dynamical system identification and approximation grounded in data fidelity. This injection of energy impacts both the dynamics of inflation and the subsequent post-inflationary universe. This work demonstrates that such features can be represented as scalar fields with K\"{a}hler non-linearities. a pivotal advancement in understanding the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity in cuprate superconductors. This study presents an ab initio study of the CuO$_2$ plane within a cuprate microscopic environment, specifically focusing on La$_2$CuO$_4$, a prototypical high-temperature superconductor. The approach utilizes a temperature-dependent tight-binding model for CuO$_2$ planes supported by one-dimensional chains of La-O-La chains, derived from ab initio calculations. These observations enable the construction of a reduced model featuring only Cu and O sites, accompanied by a quantitative analysis of the orbital content within the $c$-axis direction. The results indicate an anti-bonding configuration between Cu $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and O $p_\pi$ orbitals in the CuO$_2$ plane, alongside a bond angle distortion between La-O-La chains caused by $p_\sigma$ orbital mixing. The Cu-O $\pi$ bond strength is calculated at 0.13 eV. The O $p_\pi$ bandwidth in the CuO$_2$ plane ranges from 3.5 to 4.5 eV. As an initial demonstration, the model successfully reproduces the near half-filling band structure of La$_2$CuO$_4$ observed in photoemission experiments. Additionally, an effective Hubbard $U$ of approximately 8 eV aligns with previous ab initio findings. The resulting band dispersion exhibits significant sensitivity to oxygen self-doping. These methodologies and perspectives are deemed applicable to other layered cuprate superconductors. Consequently, this research paves the way for a reduced-model band structure of cuprates involving $d_{x^2-y^2}$ electrons, facilitating the exploration of various many-body interactions that underpin high-temperature superconductivity.

This study examines key features of solar turbulence using high-resolution convective zone simulations, employing the "direct" approach that numerically resolves the full range of relevant scales rather than applying closures or approximations. The investigation focuses on three critical aspects of solar convection: convective energy transport, the structure of turbulent flows, and magnetoconvection. These features are analyzed in the context of solar dynamo challenges. Results indicate that simulated energy transport matches observations regarding magnitude, depth, profile shape, and latitude dependence. Furthermore, the turbulent flow shows high kinetic intensity with a superconvective component in the outer convection zone. Within magnetoconvection, there is strong energy transfer from turbulence to magnetic fields, primarily through tilting of horizontal turbulent motions by mean stratified turbulence. This energy transfer is most prominent in low Prandtl number simulations and occurs in a thin layer at the convective-radiative transition zone, consistent with helioseismology observations of granular energy dissipation. These findings suggest that approximations or closures designed to represent solar turbulence in astrophysical dynamo simulations must accurately replicate these observed features. Finally, we explore how these results inform various challenges regarding solar and stellar dynamos. We conclude that direct numerical simulations are capable of providing fundamental and quantitative insights into physical processes and their impact on different scenarios. Consequently, we advocate for a shift away from relying solely on closures or approximations, arguing that direct simulations should be prioritized for investigating fundamental turbulence effects. This approach offers the opportunity to fully exploit current and upcoming supercomputer capabilities. We propose that direct simulations represent a vital step toward eventually addressing the longstanding and complex problems surrounding astrophysical turbulence. We also examine specific examples of how direct simulations can yield unambiguous results. Additionally, we emphasize the necessity of establishing quantifiable criteria for comparing numerical methods and assessing their reliability. We recommend that future research incorporating direct simulations into existing solar and stellar dynamo models explicitly quantifies the turbulence type and characteristics they simulate. Finally, we advocate for further investigation into the most appropriate simulation method based on specific physical conditions and the particular problem being addressed. To support this assertion, we theoretically examine the interaction of guided atoms with the inhomogeneous gravitational field surrounding Earth's surface. Specifically, we analyze the potential impact of tidal field gradients on the coherence of the matter-wave phase space when atoms move through it. Our demonstration reveals that standard textbook predictions, which assume spatial uniformity, lead to unphysical conclusions. Instead, we show that the spatial variation of the tidal field causes guided atoms to acquire wavepacket angular momentum as they translate. We further examine how this generated angular momentum evolves and how it transforms during the multi-wavepacket state transitions typical of advanced interferometric setups. Consequently, the temporal evolution of the two-wavepacket state coherence is influenced not only by tidal field-induced phase fluctuations, as conventionally believed, but also by the spreading and angular momentum characteristics of the local guided atoms. Finally, we outline strategies to mitigate these effects and suggest experimental parameters essential for conducting a precise measurement of the phenomenon. In summary, we establish that precise atom interferometry necessitates a rigorous treatment of atoms as polarizable dipoles moving through inhomogeneous gravitational fields. Such an approach is fundamental to both the development and the long-term stability requirements of next-generation atom interferometric gravity gradiometers. By integrating various second-moment GPD observables—specifically the total angular momentum $J_q$ carried by quarks, GPD-related form factors, and average parton transverse transverse separation—researchers can derive the twist-two flavor-separated spin-orbit correlation (SOC). This correlation metric quantifies the average correlation between a nucleon's spin and orbital angular momenta as probed by partons of a specific flavor. We contrast several existing SOC definitions found in literature, determining that only one aligns with fundamental physical principles such as Lorentz and flavor flavor symmetry. Furthermore, we establish that all valid SOC definitions are inherently connected to the GPD $H(G)$. Our findings indicate that SOC varies with the twist of the operator under study. Specifically, utilizing GPDs at twist-2, we observe a negative SOC in the nucleon, implying that orbital angular momenta associated with lower spin states of a given quantum number occur more frequently than those with higher spin states. The magnitude of this effect in the quark sector is sensitive to the specific definition of SOC employed. Additionally, we demonstrate that GPD-based SOC serves as a valuable tool for narrowing down functional forms of GPDs. Finally, we address recent discussions regarding SOC at higher GPD Fock states (twist-3 and beyond) and their significance. We show that no definition of quark-level SOC at twist-3 can simultaneously satisfy both Lorentz and flavor symmetry constraints. However, while gary-level SOC fails to be defined at higher twists, hadron-level SOC retains a natural physical interpretation. Consequently, we propose a future experimental program designed to map all relevant GPDs via SOC measurements at various Fock states. Such an effort would provide unprecedented, high-precision access to GPDs through novel observables and open a new window for exploring GPD physics. Such a program is critical for fully elucidating the complete GPD picture, including all higher-twist components. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these findings and their potential relationship to the recently discovered strange metallic phase in heavy fermion systems. Warped geometry on worldvolumes may represent an intrinsic feature of strong backreaction between worldvolume and bulk degrees of freedom, thereby establishing a natural duality with nonrelativistic CFTs. We present evidence supporting this possibility, highlighting warped CFTs as a novel class of nonrelativistic theories. Notably, a model of a single chiral fermion in two dimensions emerges as such a warped CFT, featuring a Fermi velocity that can be interpreted as an independent scale governing the underlying physics. This provides a fresh perspective on the enigmatic behavior of heavy fermion metals exhibiting non-Fermi liquid characteristics. Additionally, our analysis suggests a generalized version of the Landau Fermi liquid paradigm, applicable to both this model and other nonrelativistic CFTs. We also investigate the gravitational dual of this model and demonstrate that it aligns with a black hole scenario in an asymptotically warped AdS$_3$ geometry, consistent with earlier observations. Finally, we offer an alternative derivation of the $\frac{c}{24}$ contribution to holographic entanglement entropy from large black hole states, without relying on universal central charge considerations. This result elucidates the $24 \times \frac{s_Q}{s}$ term in QNC$_{\rm UNIV}$, a recently identified contribution to holographic entanglement entropy in quantum critical systems. We contend that this term offers a more accurate characterization of universal thermodynamic properties in large quantum systems than previously noted. Additionally, we provide an alternative derivation of this result using quantum information theory and quantum error correction, elucidating the underlying mechanisms. This insight may hold broader significance regarding the nature of holographic entanglement entropy in brane setups. Finally, we return to the heavy fermion paradigm, applying momentum-dependent finite temperature Green's functions to calculate quasi-particle densities and compare them against field theory calculations, thereby deepening our understanding of warped black holes and their properties. We also examine warped AdS$_3$ black hole thermodynamics and compare it with heavy fermion data, suggesting that warped black holes may play a crucial role in the physics of heavy fermion materials. We anticipate that these findings will stimulate further research into the connections between heavy fermion physics and warped AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ duality

Although recent advancements utilize deep representations of either kernel data or observations to address high-dimensional data, these approaches often fail to capture long-term dependencies or ensure efficient inference. This paper introduces Deep Spatial Structured GPs (DSS-GP), a novel architecture designed for data with arbitrary dimensions. In DSS-GP, GP covariance structures are learned through conditional random walk-based convolutional kernels applied to a deep Graph Convolutional Network (GCN). This method models node similarities based on the graph's structural topology, defined by an adjacency matrix derived from input features, rather than utilizing pre-defined spatial coordinates. The resulting GP covariance matrices enhance the capture of long-range dependencies while maintaining efficient inference capabilities. Empirical results confirm that DSS-GP outperforms both GPs with standard RBF kernels and those employing recently deep-learned covariandes based on Euclidean distances. Additionally, DSS-GP surpasses DGCNs on tasks involving full graph node classification and partial graph node prediction by more accurately modeling node similarities and relationships. Induced Backgrounds (BIB) caused by in-flight muon decays along the beam line, which will far surpass the levels seen at the LHC. These BIB particles will generate extensive hadronic and electromagnetic showers within the detector, severely compromising energy and momentum measurements, as well as other physics observables. Consequently, the viable detection and measurement strategies for the muon collider will differ substantially from those currently used at the LHC. This paper offers a preliminary assessment of the challenges posed by BIB to energy measurements, incorporating energy resolution, resolution uniformity across momentum and angular spectra, and the ability to identify and measure Standard Model particles with masses under 1 GeV/c². It also proposes strategies to mitigate BIB impacts, which are essential for developing a comprehensive experimental framework for muon colliders. Ultimately, determining the optimal method to manage BIB is crucial for enabling physics studies at muon colliders. To conclude, the viability of the muon collider as a Higgs factory and Higgs laboratory, as well as for top quark and top quonium studies, relies fundamentally on the solutions found for BIB within each specific detector concept. Furthermore, addressing BIB is pivotal for the muon collider's role in the broader physics program regarding charged lepton flavor violation. While a detailed analysis will require collaborative effort across collaboration groups and beyond, initiating this discussion well in advance of any muon collider decision is imperative. Such early engagement ensures that the complete detection and measurement program can be evaluated and optimized from the very beginning of the design phase. Additionally, an early understanding of BIB challenges and mitigation techniques is critical for facilitating timely studies of Higgs physics and other related processes. At the TeV energy scale, BIB represents a substantial issue that must be resolved well before the final design freeze. Delays in addressing this problem could impose a multi-year delay on the overall muon collider timeline. Therefore, it is imperative to initiate a detailed study of BIB challenges and mitigation approaches across all detector concepts at an early stage. Any delay in launching this investigation could potentially postpone the start of muon collider studies. Without prior knowledge of the specific detection and measurement capabilities of each concept, it is challenging to assess whether any single design is optimally suited to handle the extensive BIB expected at a muon collider. fundamental to explaining the diverse behaviors observed in materials. A notable example is the transition from localized Mott insulating phases in three dimensions to metallic or insonic phases in two dimensions as interaction strength increases. Nevertheless, the impact of interactions on the single-particle density of states remains poorly understood within both interacting and non-interacting systems. This study examines the connection between interactions, the density of states, and dimensionality by analyzing a single non-interacting bubble within two dimensions. Contrary to the standard single-particle parabolic dispersion form $E(k) \propto k^2$, we find that the energy dispersion relates to the square root of the density of states, yielding a form $E(k) \propto r^2$ where $r \propto k^2$. We demonstrate that this relationship remains robust across various non-interacting models and, surprisingly, persists in weakly interacting systems by introducing an $r^2$-independent parameter to extend the Peierls argument to many-body scenarios. These findings offer a novel avenue for both theoretical and experimental research. As an initial application, we show that increasing two-dimensional interaction strength smoothly shifts a system from a single-non-interacting insulating bubble to a single-particulate super-insulator. This progression is marked by the emergence of a minimum in the density of states, at which point the $r^2$ dependence of the dispersion fails, and the super-insulating state is characterized by infinite resistance and zero charge mobility at finite temperatures. Furthermore, this finding aligns with the limit of the Generalized Ginzburg-Landau theory for charge localization. Many-body effects are seen to play a critical role in localizing charge and triggering the super-insulator-to-superconductor phase transition within the insulating phase. These insights offer deeper theoretical understanding and suggest new experimental avenues for investigating the relationship between interaction strength, the density of states, and dimensionality. Focusing on the link between $r^2$ dependence and super-insulating phases, this research holds potential for advancing the field of super-insulators and the search for room-temperature super-insulator states. Additionally, the proposed methodology for incorporating many-body effects into single-particle excitations may prove valuable in exploring the relationship between the density of states and dimensionality. Finally, the current methodology for linking $r^2$ dependence to super-insulator phases can be applied to other systems to investigate how the density of states and dimensionality influence phase transitions. We express the fundamental solution using both H-function and R-function. This study investigates various graph embedding techniques, including both neural and non-neural approaches, across different network types characterized by variations in degree distribution, transitivity, and average path length. Although these methods have yielded substantial performance gains, current techniques typically rely on loosely defined similarity structures or fail to capture intricate correlations between inputs and their labels. To tackle this limitation, we introduce a novel unsupervised deep feature extraction approach named the similarity-based deep network. This method models a precise similarity pattern defined by a graph over input data, where edges denote either an unsupervised similarity relationship or a cluster assigned via a specific criterion, such as shared correlation coefficients across a set of inputs featuring multi-dimensional labels. We derive a straightforward yet effective algorithm for training networks that encode such similarity patterns, demonstrating a substantial reduction in training epochs needed to achieve high embedding quality. Finally, we evaluate this methodology across various applications, including both unsupervised and supervised contexts. Our empirical results indicate that leveraging detailed similarity patterns significantly enhances feature extraction quality both theoretically and practically. The proposed unsupervised deep feature extraction has already delivered remarkable outcomes on multi-variate time series and co-occurrence data. Furthermore, our supervised applications have attained state-of-the-art performance on the SK-ID identity co-occurrence dataset and COCO image retrieval benchmarks. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/zhongyq1991/SimDeep.

is a common challenge in fields like economics and public health. A key obstacle is ensuring valid and precise causal inference when only a fraction of units receive the treatment. This paper presents a unified framework for inference within multi-interventional networked environments. We begin by introducing a general multi-interventional multi-output setting, establishing necessary conditions for valid causal inference and presenting estimation techniques. Next, we specialize this framework to homogeneous and heterogeneous homogeneous networks, focusing on local inference. We derive identification and consistency conditions for both observation-based and interaction-based methods, alongside their corresponding estimators. Finally, we provide estimation procedures for heterogeneous networks where units are unique and possess distinct features, allowing treatment effects to vary based on these unit-specific characteristics. Numerical simulations are included to demonstrate the performance of these estimators. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the proposed estimators are robust, maintaining robustness even when specific assumptions are relaxed. These findings support the development of more effective policy interventions. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of our framework to real-world networks, including those involving political candidates and other multi-interventional scenarios. Driven by recent applications in cosmology, there is a growing need for enhanced performance in estimating the probability density function (pdf) of excursion sets. This paper introduces two novel estimators for the pdf of the minimum within compact regions of a multivariate random vector, specifically designed for cosmological microlensing data. These estimators are particularly effective for "heavy-tailed" random vectors characterized by finite variance but an undefined pdf in the tails. They are validated using synthetic data generated from a non-linear stochastic differential equation with a known analytical solution. Current estimations of the clustering index for the large-scale structure in cosmological microlensing data are significantly influenced by noise. The proposed methods suggest a straightforward strategy for noise suppression. Current analyses indicate that, after filtering, the clustering index constraint will be improved by approximately one order of magnitude. Furthermore, the paper concludes with new predictions regarding how this clustering signal evolves over time. Additionally, an open-source Python package implementing these estimators is provided.

We propose a parametric representation for the distribution function of the supremum of a centered, anisotropic, stationary, and inhomogeneous Gaussian random field, provided the field's anisotropy does not increase as the distance from the origin increases. This model offers significant potential for further statistical investigation of excursion set properties. Specifically, we demonstrate that the covariance function of a related random field vanishes more rapidly at large distances than under the standard Gaussian model. We also examine a specific instance of this model applicable to a spherically symmetric Gaussian random field and evaluate its performance using a numerically generated field with superhorizon scales. Our findings indicate that the model fits the data well, with results suggesting it may outperform existing models. We further apply the model to reduce noise in an anisotropic Gaussian random field model derived from recent cosmological data. Finally, we apply the model to analyze the clustering index of a non-Gaussian random field with heavy tails, derived from a Gaussian field via a non-linear transformation. In this scenario, the model successfully filters noisy data, leading to a substantial improvement in the precision of the estimated clustering index.

To address this, we introduce a class of random walks designed to incorporate network weights, yielding corresponding index measures for both single nodes and the network as a whole. Specifically, we derive and prove a closed-form expression for betweenness centrality in terms of edge weights and a directedness parameter. Finally, in the context of weighted networks where every node pair is connected, we identify critical edges for a node based on our derived index. To address this, we introduce an automated method that simultaneously solves two challenges: (a) finding the optimal match between sources in different catalogsues, and (b) identifying cases where no match exists. This is achieved by evaluating various physical attributes, such as uncertainties in right ascension and declination, flux, and color, while explicitly accounting for the fact that these quantities are drawn from probability distributions. We incorporate priors on source populations derived from completeness studies. The algorithm yields a specific match probability for each potential pairing and a dispersion representing the uncertainty in selecting the best candidate. A straightforward decision rule enables the selection of optimal matches and the detection of spurious ones. This automatic matching algorithm (AMA) was tested on a sample of \textit{Spitzer} IRAC 3.6 $\mu$m sources cross-referenced with 2MASS J, H, and K$_S$ band data. Our results indicate that the AMA correctly identifies approximately 96.5\% of true matches and 93.5\% of spurious matches within the source sample. The primary reason for misclassifying true matches as spurious is excessive error estimates, which are likely caused by inaccurate variance assessments in the source positions. Ultimately, we processed a dataset comprising 241,408 \textit{Spitzer} 3.6 $\mu$m sources and 1,284,673 2MASS K$_S$ sources, generating 2,010,000 unique cross-matches with a 96.5\% confidence level. Utilizing the output of the AMA significantly reduces the time required for iterative visual inspection during final verification. The source data and results are accessible at \url{http://www.astro.ucla.edu/\textit{~}kurt}/AMA/}. Additionally, we provide a free software package that implements the AMA algorithm. This paper addresses the difficulty of identifying and eliminating false positives in unsupervised machine learning contexts. We introduce Unsupervised Clean Training (UCT), a two-stage framework: i) selectively discarding easy samples from the target domain that fall outside the source domain's receptive field using an unsupervised domain alignment method, and ii) iteratively removing samples that continue to generate false positives on validation data by training a binary classifier on the selected domain. This classifier distinguishes between true positives (which produce bounding boxes) and remaining false positives. The process repeats until no false positives are present in the model's output box distribution over the validation set. UCT is model-agnostic and can be integrated with various detectors, including those used in prior domain adaptive studies. Experiments on cityscapes and Mapillary datasets demonstrate that UCT effectively eliminates false positives in unsupervised settings, achieving state-of-the-art results on the pedestrian domain of Citydiversity. The method surpasses previous detection performance and significantly reduces false positives, producing cleaner bounding boxes that are more suitable for downstream applications. This study demonstrates that various grammar decoding algorithms can be effectively approximated by an neural network specifically trained to decode a grammar defined by an English treebank. Leveraging this approximation, we demonstrate that an syntax-aware translation model significantly enhances translation quality compared to a standard beam search model. Specifically, our syntax-aware approach either mitigates common NMT errors or generates novel, more appropriate target phrases. To our knowledge, this marks the initial effort to achieve syntax-aware translation by integrating hand-crafted grammars into NMT systems. Although syntax-based decoding was previously proposed to regulate left-to-right incremental translation, our syntax-aware technique produces a completely different translation output distinct from those traditional methods. We provide a comprehensive experimental validation of hand-crafted grammar decoding and decoding algorithm approximation, both of which yield promising results. Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jianjiansc/NMT-Syntax-Aware-Decoding. Consequently, we can conclude that hand-crafted grammar decoding is feasible and that an syntax-aware translation model delivers superior performance. This research is a revised version of a paper originally accepted for publication at EMNLP 2017. Additional details are provided in the complete version available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.04873. The primary contributions of this work include the novel hand-crafted grammar decoding method and the novel syntax-aware translation model, both of which deliver superior results. Additional contributions involve a unified framework for decoding with hand-crafted grammars, a method to constrain the decoding process to ensure graph connectivity, and a novel syntax-aware translation model. Additionally, we demonstrate how to effectively integrate an existing grammar into an NMT system. Finally, we offer an implementation of hand-crafted grammar decoding available at https://github.com/jianjiansc/NMT-Syntax-Aware-Decoding. Our sources are based on Google's Sarama, and we have introduced several modifications to better support hand-crafted grammar decoding. To our knowledge, this is the first implementation of hand-crafted grammar decoding for NMT. This implementation supports both CFG and PEG grammars, although only CFG decoding is detailed in this paper. Additionally, we provide a method to conveniently integrate an existing grammar into an NMT system using existing tools. Finally, we demonstrate how to visualize parse trees generated by both the parser and the decoder.

Quantization and model pruning are two primary methods for compressing neural networks, though prior research has predominantly focused their compression research on English. This study investigates the effectiveness of applying quantization and pruning to multilingual models for machine translation. Although initial findings indicate that these compression techniques perform comparably on English, experiments across various languages reveal significant quality degradation when applied to models trained on English alone. To address this, the paper examines the impact of diverse pretraining conditions and demonstrates that utilizing a combined pretraining corpus—incorporating data from multiple languages alongside English—substantially enhances translation performance following compression. This improvement suggests that such models are more robust to both quantization and pruning. Ultimately, the research concludes that engaging heavily with non-English corpora during pretraining benefits not only compressed models but also their uncompressed counterparts. Empirically, this insight challenges the conventional machine translation paradigm that prioritizes English exclusively during pretraining. By adopting a more inclusive pretraining strategy, massively multilingual models can achieve major performance gains without increasing model size. Additionally, this approach enables the use of significantly smaller models trained solely on English, overcoming the computational and memory constraints associated with their prior usage. A longstanding conjecture by Erd\\"os, Faudree, Shastri, and Tajshidarian, building on specific cases established by Faudree, Shastri, and Soltan, posits that for any two-partite graph $F$ with maximum degree $\Delta(F)=d$, the Tur\'an number behaves asymptotically as $Tur_{2}(F) = (1 - \frac{1}{d-1})\binom{n}{2} + o(n^2)$. In this paper, we confirm a significant portion of this conjecture and demonstrate a constructive lower bound for $Tur_{2}(F)$ that matches the proposed asymptotic bound whenever $F$ contains a $K_{d+1}$ as a subgraph. This study addresses these issues by demonstrating that combining self-training with data augmentation yields significant advancements in the automated study of bone morphology. Although end-to-end neural approaches have demonstrated promising results, they remain vulnerable to the inherent limitations of ASR systems. This study explores whether we can leverage reliable ASR systems to enhance the performance of end-to-end ST models. We utilize a widely accepted ST benchmark and state-of-the-art models to compare three distinct architectures: Asynchronous Fused Encoder, Parallel Encoder, and Cross Encoder. These variants of the same architecture are trained in an end-to-end framework, with the variations arising from how they integrate with ASR systems. Our findings indicate that ASR information serves as an effective encoder for end-to-end ST models, yielding performance gains of up to 10 BLEU points. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an encoder designed to capture long-range dependencies within speech signals yields superior results compared to one focusing on shorter-range dependencies. Finally, we present insights into the most effective combination of resources and architectures to achieve an optimal ST system. In terms of performance, the Parallel Encoder utilizing ASR information performed best, followed by the Cross Encoder using the same resource. However, considering the balance between performance and training time, the Asynchronous Fused Encoder using ASR information emerged as the most efficient model, achieving an improvement of up to 5 BLEU points compared to any other evaluated model.
